sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Late Cretaceous was the final epoch of the Mesozoic era, spanning from about 100.5 to 66 million years ago. It represents the culmination of the Age of Dinosaurs, when some of the most famous prehistoric animals — including Tyrannosaurus, Triceratops, and the duck-billed hadrosaurs — roamed the continents.

The epoch was a time of high sea levels, warm global temperatures, and continued fragmentation of the continents. Flowering plants, which had appeared in the Early Cretaceous, rose to ecological dominance, transforming landscapes and forging new relationships with insect pollinators.

The Late Cretaceous ended abruptly with the K-Pg mass extinction, triggered by the Chicxulub asteroid impact. This catastrophe brought an end to the non-avian dinosaurs and many other groups, closing a chapter of Earth's history that had lasted more than 180 million years [1].

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
The early part of the Late Cretaceous was among the warmest intervals of the past quarter-billion years. During the Cenomanian and Turonian stages, around 94 to 90 million years ago, tropical sea surface temperatures may have exceeded 35 °C, and polar regions were free of permanent ice [2]. Forests grew at high latitudes in both hemispheres, and crocodile relatives lived in the Canadian Arctic.

Atmospheric carbon dioxide levels were several times higher than today, sustained by vigorous volcanic activity and high rates of seafloor spreading. The Cenomanian–Turonian boundary was marked by Oceanic Anoxic Event 2, during which large areas of the ocean floor became starved of oxygen, leading to widespread burial of organic-rich black shales [2].

From the Turonian onward, the climate underwent a gradual cooling trend that continued through the Campanian and Maastrichtian stages. Even so, the world of the latest Cretaceous remained far warmer than the present, with mild conditions extending to high latitudes and only seasonal frost near the poles [2].

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
Sea levels during the Late Cretaceous reached some of the highest values of the Phanerozoic, perhaps 100 to 250 metres above today's levels [3]. Shallow epicontinental seas flooded large parts of the continents. In North America, the Western Interior Seaway stretched from the Gulf of Mexico to the Arctic Ocean, dividing the continent into two landmasses: Laramidia in the west and Appalachia in the east.

The supercontinent of Gondwana continued to break apart. South America and Africa had fully separated, widening the South Atlantic, while India drifted rapidly northward as an island continent after splitting from Madagascar. Australia and Antarctica remained joined, and Europe existed largely as an archipelago of islands scattered across a warm, shallow sea.

Toward the end of the epoch, mountain building began along the western margin of North America in an episode known as the Laramide orogeny, which would eventually raise the Rocky Mountains. Meanwhile, the great flood basalts of the Deccan Traps began to erupt in western India shortly before the close of the Cretaceous.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
The Late Cretaceous witnessed the rise of flowering plants, or angiosperms, from a minor component of plant communities to the dominant group in many ecosystems. By the end of the epoch, angiosperms made up the majority of plant species in many regions, although conifers still dominated the canopies of many forests and remained especially important at higher latitudes.

Many modern plant families appeared or diversified during this time, including early relatives of magnolias, laurels, sycamores, palms, and water lilies. Deciduous trees became common in the seasonal high-latitude forests, where they shed their leaves to survive months of polar darkness. Grasses may have made their first appearance, as suggested by grass phytoliths found in fossilised dinosaur dung from India [4].

The spread of angiosperms had profound ecological consequences. Their fast growth and efficient reproduction supported new kinds of herbivores, and their flowers and fruits coevolved with insects such as bees, butterflies, and beetles, establishing pollination partnerships that remain central to terrestrial ecosystems today.

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
Late Cretaceous seas teemed with life. Mosasaurs — giant marine lizards related to modern monitor lizards and snakes — became the apex predators of the oceans, some exceeding 15 metres in length. Long-necked elasmosaurid plesiosaurs, sea turtles such as Archelon, and large predatory fish like Xiphactinus shared these waters. Ammonites remained abundant and diverse, including bizarre heteromorph forms with uncoiled shells, while rudist bivalves built extensive reef-like structures in tropical seas.

In the skies, pterosaurs reached their largest sizes. Azhdarchids such as Quetzalcoatlus had wingspans of around 10 metres and may have stalked prey on the ground like giant storks. Birds were diverse, including toothed seabirds such as Hesperornis and Ichthyornis, as well as the enantiornithines and early members of the modern bird lineage.

On land, mammals remained generally small but were more diverse than often assumed. Multituberculates, early marsupial relatives, and placental relatives occupied a wide range of niches. Snakes, lizards, crocodylomorphs, turtles, and frogs were common, and social insects such as ants and termites were becoming established.

sections.heading: Dinosaur Evolution
sections.body:
The Late Cretaceous was a golden age of dinosaur diversity. In Asia and North America, tyrannosaurids evolved into enormous apex predators, culminating in Tyrannosaurus rex, one of the largest land carnivores of all time. In the southern continents, abelisaurids such as Carnotaurus and Majungasaurus filled similar roles, while giant carcharodontosaurids had largely disappeared early in the epoch.

Herbivorous dinosaurs developed sophisticated feeding adaptations. Hadrosaurs possessed dental batteries containing hundreds of tightly packed teeth for grinding tough plant material, and many sported elaborate hollow crests used for display and vocal communication. Ceratopsians, including Triceratops and Styracosaurus, developed spectacular horns and frills, while heavily armoured ankylosaurids carried bony tail clubs.

Sauropods were rare in North America for much of the epoch but thrived in the southern continents, where titanosaurs such as Argentinosaurus and Patagotitan reached lengths of more than 30 metres. Small feathered theropods — including dromaeosaurs like Velociraptor, troodontids, and the beaked oviraptorosaurs — highlighted the close evolutionary relationship between dinosaurs and birds.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The mid-Cretaceous is an informal term used for the interval spanning roughly the Albian and Cenomanian stages, from about 113 to 94 million years ago, bridging the Early and Late Cretaceous epochs. It is remembered as one of the warmest times in Earth's history and as a period of intense geological and biological change.

During this time, a pulse of volcanic activity and rapid seafloor spreading drove atmospheric carbon dioxide to very high levels, producing a 'greenhouse world' with no permanent polar ice. Sea levels rose dramatically, and the oceans repeatedly became starved of oxygen in episodes known as Oceanic Anoxic Events [1, 2].

Biologically, the mid-Cretaceous is marked by the rapid spread of flowering plants and by a turnover in dinosaur faunas, as giant predators such as Spinosaurus and Giganotosaurus reached their peak and the lineages that would dominate the Late Cretaceous began to emerge.

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
The mid-Cretaceous climate was exceptionally hot. The interval culminated in the Cretaceous Thermal Maximum near the Cenomanian–Turonian boundary, when tropical sea surface temperatures may have reached 35 °C or more and deep ocean waters were perhaps 15 to 20 °C warmer than today. Atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations were several times higher than pre-industrial levels [2].

The temperature gradient between the equator and the poles was much weaker than in the modern world. Polar regions experienced mild, temperate climates, supporting forests and a variety of reptiles and dinosaurs well within the Arctic and Antarctic circles. Winters at high latitudes were dark but rarely severe enough to sustain permanent ice.

This warm world was punctuated by episodes of oceanic oxygen depletion. Oceanic Anoxic Events 1b and 1d occurred during the Albian, and the pronounced Oceanic Anoxic Event 2 took place at the Cenomanian–Turonian boundary. These events buried vast quantities of organic carbon in deep-sea sediments, forming many of the world's important petroleum source rocks [1, 2].

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
The mid-Cretaceous saw a remarkable episode of tectonic activity. Massive submarine volcanic plateaus, such as the Ontong Java and Kerguelen plateaus, were formed by enormous outpourings of basaltic lava, and mid-ocean ridges spread at unusually rapid rates. This swelling of the ocean floor displaced seawater onto the continents, driving sea levels to some of their highest values in the last 500 million years [1].

The South Atlantic Ocean was widening as South America and Africa completed their separation, with the final marine connection between the North and South Atlantic established around 100 million years ago. India, Madagascar, and the Antarctic–Australian block were drifting apart, and the Tethys Ocean still separated the northern continents from Africa.

In North America, the Western Interior Seaway began to take shape as marine waters flooded southward from the Arctic and northward from the Gulf of Mexico, eventually splitting the continent in two. Much of Europe and North Africa lay beneath shallow tropical seas, where thick deposits of chalk and limestone began to accumulate.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
The mid-Cretaceous is the interval during which flowering plants underwent their first great expansion. Having originated as small, weedy plants in disturbed habitats earlier in the Cretaceous, angiosperms diversified rapidly during the Albian and Cenomanian, spreading across the globe and occupying a growing range of ecological niches.

Early angiosperm forests included relatives of modern magnolias, laurels, and plane trees, and the first eudicots — the group that today includes most flowering plants — became widespread. Water lilies and other aquatic angiosperms colonised lakes and rivers, while flowering shrubs and herbs spread along floodplains and in the understorey of conifer-dominated forests.

Despite this expansion, conifers such as araucarians and cheirolepidiaceans, together with ferns, cycads, and ginkgos, remained important components of most plant communities. Amber deposits from this period, such as those from northern Myanmar, preserve exquisite details of the forest ecosystems, including flowers, insects, spiders, small lizards, and even feathered dinosaur tails.

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
Mid-Cretaceous oceans were home to a rich variety of marine reptiles. Ichthyosaurs survived into the late Cenomanian before finally going extinct [3], while short-necked pliosaurs and long-necked plesiosaurs remained common. The first mosasaurs appeared toward the end of this interval, beginning an evolutionary radiation that would make them the dominant marine predators of the Late Cretaceous.

Invertebrate life flourished in the warm, shallow seas. Ammonites were abundant, rudist bivalves formed extensive reef-like buildups, and planktonic foraminifera and coccolithophores diversified, the latter contributing to vast chalk deposits. Early modern sharks and ray-finned fishes continued to diversify.

On land, the spread of flowering plants was accompanied by a diversification of insects, including early bees, moths, and pollinating beetles. Lizards, snakes, crocodylomorphs, and turtles were widespread, and mammals — including early relatives of placentals and marsupials — scurried through the undergrowth. In the skies, pterosaurs such as the toothed ornithocheirids soared over the seas alongside a growing diversity of birds.

sections.heading: Dinosaur Evolution
sections.body:
The mid-Cretaceous was the heyday of some of the largest predatory dinosaurs ever to live. In South America, the carcharodontosaurid Giganotosaurus rivalled or exceeded Tyrannosaurus in length, while in North Africa, the sail-backed Spinosaurus — likely a semi-aquatic fish eater — shared river systems with Carcharodontosaurus and a host of other large predators, a remarkable concentration of carnivores recorded in the Kem Kem beds of Morocco [4].

Giant titanosaurian sauropods thrived in the southern continents; Argentinosaurus, which lived around 95 million years ago, may have been one of the heaviest land animals of all time. In the northern continents, iguanodontian ornithopods and nodosaurid ankylosaurs were common herbivores.

This interval also saw the emergence of groups that would dominate the Late Cretaceous. Early tyrannosauroids remained relatively small, but lineages leading to the giant tyrannosaurids were present in Asia and North America. The first hadrosauroids and neoceratopsians were diversifying, setting the stage for the great herds of duck-billed and horned dinosaurs that followed.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Early Cretaceous was the first epoch of the Cretaceous period, lasting from about 145 to 100.5 million years ago. At more than 40 million years, it is one of the longest epochs in the geological timescale, and it witnessed some of the most important events in the history of life, including the origin and early diversification of flowering plants.

The epoch was characterised by the continued break-up of the supercontinent Pangaea. The southern landmass of Gondwana began to split apart, opening the South Atlantic and Indian oceans and increasingly isolating the faunas of different continents.

Dinosaurs remained the dominant land animals, but the Early Cretaceous saw a changing of the guard, as many of the giant sauropods of the Jurassic declined in the north and new groups of herbivores and feathered theropods rose to prominence. Exceptionally preserved fossils from sites such as the Jehol Biota of China have revealed an astonishing diversity of feathered dinosaurs, early birds, and mammals [1].

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
The climate of the Early Cretaceous was generally warm, although it was cooler and more variable than the extreme greenhouse of the mid-Cretaceous. At the beginning of the epoch, conditions were relatively cool compared with the rest of the period, and there is evidence of seasonal ice at high latitudes, including glacial dropstones and glendonite crystals in Arctic and Australian sediments [2].

Through the epoch, temperatures gradually rose, driven by increasing volcanic activity and rising atmospheric carbon dioxide. The Aptian stage was marked by Oceanic Anoxic Event 1a, around 120 million years ago, linked to the massive eruptions that formed the Ontong Java Plateau in the Pacific. This event caused widespread oxygen depletion in the oceans and disrupted marine ecosystems.

Climate zones were broader than today, with arid belts extending across the interiors of the continents and humid, warm-temperate forests flourishing at higher latitudes. Southern Australia, then located near the South Pole, experienced cool, seasonally dark conditions, yet still supported dinosaurs adapted to polar life.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
During the Early Cretaceous, the ongoing fragmentation of Pangaea accelerated. Gondwana began to separate into its component parts: rifting between South America and Africa opened the southern South Atlantic, leaving behind extensive rift lakes and salt deposits along the future continental margins. Meanwhile, India and Madagascar broke away from Antarctica and Australia, beginning the opening of the Indian Ocean.

In the north, Laurasia remained partially connected, but the North Atlantic continued to widen, and shallow seas periodically flooded parts of Europe, creating an archipelago of islands. The Tethys Ocean separated Laurasia from Africa and extended as a broad seaway across the tropics.

Sea levels generally rose during the epoch as rates of seafloor spreading increased. Large volcanic provinces formed, including the Paraná–Etendeka Traps, which erupted as South America and Africa separated, and the Ontong Java Plateau, one of the largest volcanic features on Earth. These events had important effects on global climate and ocean chemistry.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
The Early Cretaceous is the time when flowering plants, or angiosperms, first appear clearly in the fossil record. The earliest definite angiosperm pollen dates to around 135 to 130 million years ago, and early flowering plants such as Archaefructus from the Jehol Biota of China and Montsechia from Spain were small, likely aquatic or semi-aquatic plants [3].

For most of the epoch, however, landscapes were dominated by more ancient plant groups. Conifers, including araucarians, podocarps, and the now-extinct cheirolepidiaceans, formed extensive forests. Ferns carpeted the ground in many habitats, and cycads, bennettitaleans, and ginkgos were widespread. Horsetails grew along the margins of rivers and lakes.

By the end of the Early Cretaceous, angiosperms had diversified considerably and begun to spread into a wider range of habitats. Their rapid life cycles and efficient reproduction allowed them to colonise disturbed environments such as floodplains, setting the stage for their explosive rise to dominance later in the Cretaceous.

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
Early Cretaceous ecosystems were rich and varied. Lake deposits such as those of the Jehol Biota in northeastern China and Las Hoyas in Spain preserve entire communities in remarkable detail, including insects, fish, salamanders, frogs, turtles, lizards, and choristoderes — aquatic reptiles resembling crocodiles [1].

Mammals were diverse and more ecologically varied than once thought. Repenomamus, a badger-sized mammal from China, was found with the remains of a juvenile dinosaur in its stomach, demonstrating that some Mesozoic mammals preyed on small dinosaurs [4]. Early members of the lineages leading to placentals and marsupials also appeared during this time.

In the seas, ichthyosaurs, plesiosaurs, and pliosaurs remained important predators, while ammonites, belemnites, and bivalves were abundant. Pterosaurs diversified into a variety of forms, including the filter-feeding Pterodaustro, and the toothed, crested ornithocheirids that soared over the oceans. Early birds such as Confuciusornis and a variety of enantiornithines shared the skies with them.

sections.heading: Dinosaur Evolution
sections.body:
The Early Cretaceous saw a major reorganisation of dinosaur communities. In the Northern Hemisphere, the giant diplodocid and brachiosaurid sauropods of the Jurassic became rarer, and herbivorous ornithopods such as Iguanodon — one of the first dinosaurs ever described — became dominant, together with armoured nodosaurids and early ceratopsians such as Psittacosaurus.

In the Southern Hemisphere, sauropods remained important, with rebbachisaurids and early titanosaurs thriving across Gondwana. Large predatory theropods included spinosaurids such as Baryonyx, with crocodile-like snouts adapted for catching fish, and allosauroids such as Acrocanthosaurus, with its distinctive ridge of tall spines along its back.

Perhaps the most significant discoveries from the Early Cretaceous are the feathered dinosaurs of the Jehol Biota. Species such as Sinosauropteryx, Microraptor, and the early tyrannosauroid Yutyrannus preserve feathers ranging from simple filaments to fully formed flight feathers. These fossils have transformed our understanding of dinosaur biology and provided compelling evidence that birds are the living descendants of theropod dinosaurs [1].

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Late Jurassic was the final epoch of the Jurassic period, spanning from about 161.5 to 145 million years ago. It is often regarded as the iconic age of the dinosaurs, when colossal long-necked sauropods such as Brachiosaurus, Diplodocus, and Apatosaurus roamed the land alongside predators like Allosaurus and armoured herbivores like Stegosaurus.

The epoch was a time of warm, largely ice-free climates and high sea levels, as the supercontinent Pangaea continued to break apart. Shallow tropical seas covered much of Europe, providing habitats for rich marine faunas and giving rise to famous fossil deposits.

The Late Jurassic is also notable for the appearance of Archaeopteryx, the famous 'first bird', whose exquisitely preserved fossils from the Solnhofen limestone of Germany became a landmark in the understanding of evolution shortly after the publication of Darwin's On the Origin of Species.

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
The Late Jurassic climate was warm and largely free of permanent polar ice, with global average temperatures substantially higher than today. Atmospheric carbon dioxide levels were several times pre-industrial values, and the temperature difference between the equator and the poles was modest, allowing forests to grow at high latitudes [1].

There was, however, considerable regional variation. Large parts of the continental interiors, particularly in western North America and parts of Gondwana, experienced seasonally dry, semi-arid conditions, with wet and dry seasons driven by monsoonal circulation. Evidence from the Morrison Formation of the western United States suggests a landscape of open floodplains, seasonal rivers, and scattered woodlands [2].

Coastal regions and islands, such as those of the European archipelago, enjoyed warm, humid, and often subtropical climates. Some evidence suggests a modest cooling trend toward the end of the epoch, as the world transitioned into the Early Cretaceous.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
By the Late Jurassic, Pangaea was well into its break-up. The central Atlantic Ocean had opened between North America and northwest Africa, creating a widening seaway that connected the Tethys Ocean to the proto-Pacific. Laurasia to the north and Gondwana to the south were increasingly separated, although land connections likely persisted in some areas.

High sea levels caused shallow seas to flood much of Europe, which existed as an archipelago of islands surrounded by warm lagoons and carbonate platforms. Some of these lagoons, such as those around Solnhofen in Bavaria, had stagnant, hypersaline bottom waters that preserved fossils in extraordinary detail.

In western North America, the Sundance Sea retreated, and rivers draining newly uplifted highlands to the west deposited the sediments of the Morrison Formation across a broad lowland [2]. Gondwana remained largely intact, but rifting had begun along the margins that would later separate Africa, India, Antarctica, and Australia.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
The Late Jurassic flora was dominated by gymnosperms — seed plants that do not produce flowers. Conifers were the principal trees, including members of the araucarian family (relatives of today's monkey-puzzle trees), podocarps, and the extinct cheirolepidiaceans, which were particularly well adapted to warm, dry environments.

Cycads, cycad-like bennettitaleans, and ginkgos were common in many habitats, while tree ferns and ground ferns thrived in moist areas. Horsetails grew in dense stands along riverbanks and lake margins. Flowering plants had not yet appeared, and grasses would not evolve for many tens of millions of years, so open habitats were covered by ferns and low-growing shrubs rather than grassland.

The tall conifers and tree ferns provided an abundant, if tough and low-nutrient, food source for the enormous sauropods. The need to process large volumes of fibrous vegetation may have been one of the factors that favoured the evolution of gigantic body sizes in these herbivores [3].

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
Late Jurassic seas were ruled by marine reptiles. Giant pliosaurs such as Pliosaurus and Liopleurodon were apex predators with massive skulls and powerful jaws, while long-necked plesiosaurs hunted fish and cephalopods. Ichthyosaurs such as Ophthalmosaurus, with enormous eyes adapted for deep diving, were common, and marine crocodylomorphs known as metriorhynchids had evolved paddle-like limbs and tail flukes for a fully aquatic life.

Ammonites and belemnites were abundant, and reefs built by sponges and corals flourished in the warm, shallow waters of the Tethys. Bony fishes and sharks continued to diversify, including the giant filter-feeding fish Leedsichthys, one of the largest fish ever to have lived.

On land and in the air, pterosaurs were diverse, including long-tailed rhamphorhynchids and the first short-tailed pterodactyloids. Small mammals were widespread, including docodonts and early relatives of modern mammal groups, some of which were adapted for swimming, burrowing, or gliding. Lizards, turtles, crocodylomorphs, and sphenodontians also inhabited Late Jurassic ecosystems.

sections.heading: Dinosaur Evolution
sections.body:
The Late Jurassic is renowned for its giant sauropods. In North America, the Morrison Formation has yielded Diplodocus, Apatosaurus, Brontosaurus, Camarasaurus, and Brachiosaurus, while the Tendaguru beds of Tanzania preserve the towering Giraffatitan. These animals evolved long necks for reaching vegetation across wide areas, air-filled bones to reduce weight, and efficient bird-like respiratory systems [3].

The principal predators were large theropods such as Allosaurus, Torvosaurus, and Ceratosaurus, which likely preyed on juvenile sauropods and other herbivores. Among the plant-eaters, stegosaurs with their distinctive plates and spiked tails reached their peak diversity, and early ankylosaurs and small ornithopods were also present.

The epoch also marked a key stage in the evolution of birds. Archaeopteryx, from the Solnhofen limestone, combined bird-like features such as feathered wings with reptilian traits including teeth, clawed fingers, and a long bony tail. Other small feathered theropods from China, such as Anchiornis, show that feathers were widespread among the dinosaur lineage leading to birds [4].

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Mesozoic Marine Revolution was a profound and prolonged transformation of marine ecosystems that unfolded during the Mesozoic era, reaching a major phase of intensification during the Late Jurassic and Early Cretaceous, roughly 160 to 130 million years ago. Unlike a mass extinction, it was not a single catastrophic event but a gradual evolutionary escalation between predators and their prey.

The concept was first proposed by the palaeontologist Geerat Vermeij in 1977. He observed that, over the course of the Mesozoic, marine predators evolved increasingly powerful means of crushing, drilling, and prying open shells, and that their prey responded by evolving thicker, spinier, and more heavily armoured shells, or by adopting new lifestyles such as burrowing deeply into sediment [1].

The revolution fundamentally reshaped life on the seafloor, replacing many of the ancient, sedentary communities of the Paleozoic with the more mobile, defended, and predator-driven ecosystems that characterise the modern oceans.

sections.heading: Causes & Triggers
sections.body:
The driving force of the Mesozoic Marine Revolution was the evolution and diversification of new kinds of shell-breaking, or durophagous, predators. These included bony fishes with specialised crushing jaws and teeth, rays and sharks with pavement-like dental plates, and marine reptiles such as placodonts and later certain plesiosaurs and mosasaurs with blunt, rounded teeth suited to crushing shells [1].

Invertebrate predators also played a central role. Decapod crustaceans, including crabs and lobsters, evolved powerful crushing claws, while predatory snails developed the ability to drill through shells with their radula and acidic secretions. Starfish evolved the ability to pry open bivalves, and cephalopods developed beaks capable of breaking shells.

The revolution was likely fuelled by increased productivity in the warm, nutrient-rich oceans of the Jurassic and Cretaceous. The expansion of shallow epicontinental seas, rising sea levels, and the diversification of plankton increased the energy available to marine food webs, supporting larger populations of active, energy-hungry predators and intensifying the evolutionary arms race.

sections.heading: Climatic/Environmental Changes
sections.body:
The Mesozoic Marine Revolution unfolded against the backdrop of a warm greenhouse world. During the Late Jurassic and Early Cretaceous, the break-up of Pangaea created new ocean basins and extensive shallow seas along continental margins, greatly increasing the area of habitable, well-lit seafloor where the arms race between predators and prey could play out.

High rates of seafloor spreading and volcanic activity raised atmospheric carbon dioxide and sea levels, while changes in ocean chemistry favoured the production of calcium carbonate by planktonic organisms. The rise of calcareous nannoplankton, such as coccolithophores, and of planktonic foraminifera transformed the carbon cycle, shifting much carbonate deposition from shallow shelves into the deep ocean [2].

These environmental changes created new ecological opportunities. Increased nutrient supply from weathering of the continents, combined with warm temperatures, boosted primary productivity, while the growing diversity of habitats encouraged specialisation among both predators and prey.

sections.heading: Biological Impact
sections.body:
The revolution drove a dramatic shift in the composition of seafloor communities. Stalked crinoids, brachiopods, and other sedentary animals that lived exposed on the seafloor declined in shallow waters and were increasingly confined to deep-sea refuges where predation pressure was lower [3]. Their place was taken by more mobile and better-defended animals.

Many molluscs evolved new defences. Gastropods developed thicker shells, narrower apertures, spines, and ribs that made them harder to crush or drill, while bivalves evolved deeper burrowing habits, the ability to swim or cement themselves to rocks, and tightly sealing shells [1]. Some groups, such as the ammonites, evolved more ornamented and complex shells, perhaps partly in response to increased predation.

Predators themselves diversified rapidly. Modern groups of crabs, lobsters, predatory snails, teleost fishes, sharks, and rays either originated or radiated during this time. Marine reptiles also adapted to the new food sources, and the evolutionary escalation continued through the Cretaceous and into the Cenozoic.

sections.heading: Legacy
sections.body:
The Mesozoic Marine Revolution laid the foundations of the modern marine biosphere. Many of the dominant groups in today's oceans — including teleost fishes, modern crabs, predatory snails, and burrowing bivalves — owe their success to adaptations forged during this period. The ecological structure of present-day seafloor communities, with their emphasis on mobility, burrowing, and defence, is a direct legacy of this escalation.

The concept also had a lasting impact on evolutionary theory. Vermeij's work highlighted the importance of biological interactions, especially predation, as a major driver of large-scale evolutionary change, complementing the traditional focus on physical environmental factors such as climate and sea level.

The revolution is often cited as a classic example of an evolutionary arms race and of escalation, the idea that over long periods of time, enemies such as predators become more powerful and their prey become better defended. Similar patterns have since been identified in other episodes of Earth history, including the Paleozoic and Cenozoic eras [4].

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Middle Jurassic was the second of the three epochs of the Jurassic period, lasting from about 174 to 161.5 million years ago. Although historically less well known than the Early and Late Jurassic, due in part to a relative scarcity of rich fossil sites, it was a time of key evolutionary innovations and of major changes in the Earth's geography.

During this epoch, Pangaea continued to break apart, and the young central Atlantic Ocean began to widen as true oceanic crust formed between North America and Africa. The world was warm and largely ice-free, and shallow seas spread across large parts of the continents.

The Middle Jurassic saw the diversification of many of the dinosaur lineages that would dominate the later Mesozoic, including the first large tetanuran theropods, early stegosaurs, and the ancestors of the giant sauropods of the Late Jurassic. Important discoveries from China, England, and Argentina have revealed much about life during this formative interval.

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
The Middle Jurassic climate was generally warm and humid, with no permanent polar ice caps. Atmospheric carbon dioxide levels were high, and global temperatures were considerably warmer than today, although evidence from oxygen isotopes and fossil distributions suggests that temperatures fluctuated during the epoch, with some intervals of relative cooling [1].

The temperature gradient between the equator and the poles was gentle, allowing lush forests to grow at high latitudes in both hemispheres. Large parts of the continental interiors, especially in low latitudes, remained seasonally arid, while coastal regions experienced monsoonal rainfall.

The break-up of Pangaea and the development of new seaways gradually altered patterns of ocean and atmospheric circulation. The opening of the Hispanic Corridor, a narrow seaway connecting the Tethys Ocean to the eastern Pacific through the region of Central America, allowed marine waters and organisms to move between ocean basins, influencing both climate and the distribution of marine life.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
During the Middle Jurassic, the supercontinent Pangaea was in the process of splitting into two great landmasses: Laurasia in the north, comprising North America, Europe, and Asia, and Gondwana in the south, comprising South America, Africa, Antarctica, Australia, and India. Seafloor spreading in the central Atlantic began around this time, gradually pushing North America away from Africa.

In the Gulf of Mexico region, rifting created a restricted basin where seawater evaporated to form thick salt deposits, which later played an important role in the formation of oil and gas reservoirs. Extensive shallow seas covered much of Europe, depositing limestones and oolitic sediments that are now widely used as building stone in England and France.

In East Asia, large lake basins formed in what is now northern China, preserving the remarkable fossils of the Yanliao Biota. In western North America, the Sundance Sea spread southward from the Arctic, flooding parts of the continental interior.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
The vegetation of the Middle Jurassic was dominated by gymnosperms and ferns. Conifers were the principal trees of most forests, including early members of the pine, cypress, and araucarian families, as well as extinct groups such as the cheirolepidiaceans. Ginkgos were especially diverse and widespread at this time, particularly in the humid mid- to high-latitude forests of Laurasia.

Cycads and bennettitaleans — seed plants with cycad-like foliage and flower-like reproductive structures — were common in the understorey and in open habitats. Ferns, including tree ferns and ground-covering species, flourished in moist environments, while horsetails formed dense thickets along the edges of rivers and lakes.

Flowering plants had not yet appeared in the fossil record, although some scientists have proposed that their earliest ancestors may have existed during this time. The widespread, fibrous gymnosperm vegetation provided the food base for the growing diversity of herbivorous dinosaurs.

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
Middle Jurassic marine ecosystems were rich in marine reptiles. Ichthyosaurs, plesiosaurs, and increasingly large pliosaurs hunted in the oceans, while the thalattosuchian crocodylomorphs, including the first fully marine metriorhynchids, were diversifying. Ammonites and belemnites were abundant, and bivalves and brachiopods formed dense communities on the seafloor.

On land, the Middle Jurassic was a key interval in the evolution of mammals. Fossils from the Yanliao Biota of China include Castorocauda, a beaver-like swimming docodont [2], Volaticotherium, a gliding mammal, and early relatives of modern mammal groups. These discoveries show that Mesozoic mammals were far more ecologically diverse than once believed [2, 3].

Pterosaurs were well established in the skies, and the Yanliao Biota has also produced exceptionally preserved insects, salamanders, and the first known examples of many modern insect groups [3]. Lizards, turtles, and early crocodyliforms were also present in terrestrial and freshwater habitats.

sections.heading: Dinosaur Evolution
sections.body:
The Middle Jurassic was a time of significant diversification for dinosaurs. Among the theropods, the tetanurans — the group that includes allosaurs, spinosaurs, and coelurosaurs — underwent a major radiation. Megalosaurus, from the Middle Jurassic of England, was the first dinosaur ever to be scientifically named, in 1824.

Sauropods continued their evolution toward gigantic sizes. Early eusauropods such as Shunosaurus in China and Cetiosaurus in England were widespread, and the lineages leading to the diplodocids and macronarians of the Late Jurassic were emerging. Shunosaurus is notable for having a bony club at the tip of its tail, possibly used for defence.

Ornithischian dinosaurs also diversified, with early stegosaurs such as Huayangosaurus and early ankylosaurs appearing. Perhaps most significant was the appearance of small, feathered paravian dinosaurs in the Yanliao Biota, such as Anchiornis and the bizarre, bat-winged Yi qi. These fossils show that feathers and early forms of flight or gliding had evolved among the ancestors of birds by around the Middle–Late Jurassic boundary [3, 4].

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Early Jurassic was the first epoch of the Jurassic period, lasting from about 201.4 to 174 million years ago [1]. It began in the aftermath of the Triassic–Jurassic mass extinction, which removed many of the competitors of the dinosaurs and allowed them to rise to dominance on land [2].

During this epoch, Pangaea was beginning to break apart, and the rifting that would eventually open the Atlantic Ocean was well under way. The climate was warm, and shallow seas spread across the margins of the continents, preserving rich marine fossil deposits in places such as the Jurassic Coast of southern England and the Posidonia Shale of Germany.

The Early Jurassic is an important period for palaeontology. It was from rocks of this age that some of the first marine reptile fossils were discovered and described in the early nineteenth century, notably by the pioneering English fossil collector Mary Anning, whose finds of ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs helped lay the foundations of the science.

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
The Early Jurassic climate was warm and largely ice-free, although it was punctuated by significant fluctuations. Following the Triassic–Jurassic extinction, atmospheric carbon dioxide levels remained high, and global temperatures were considerably warmer than today. The interior of Pangaea remained seasonally arid, with extensive deserts in places such as the southwestern United States.

The most dramatic climatic event of the epoch was the Toarcian Oceanic Anoxic Event, around 183 million years ago. Linked to the eruptions of the Karoo–Ferrar large igneous province in southern Africa and Antarctica, it caused rapid global warming, widespread oxygen depletion in the oceans, and the deposition of organic-rich black shales across Europe and beyond [3, 4].

The Toarcian event triggered a significant extinction of marine life, particularly among bivalves, ammonites, and other invertebrates, and caused changes in terrestrial ecosystems [3]. It is often studied as an ancient analogue for the effects of rapid carbon release and ocean deoxygenation.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
At the start of the Early Jurassic, the continents were still assembled into the supercontinent Pangaea, stretching from pole to pole and surrounded by the vast ocean of Panthalassa. The Tethys Ocean formed a large embayment on its eastern side. However, rifting was already under way, particularly between North America and Africa, where the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province had erupted at the end of the Triassic.

As rifting continued, a series of basins developed along the future margins of the Atlantic, some of which filled with lakes and river sediments, while others were flooded by the sea. Sea levels rose during the epoch, and shallow marine environments spread across much of Europe, which became a patchwork of islands and shallow basins.

The desert dune fields of the Navajo Sandstone, preserved in spectacular cliffs in Utah and Arizona, represent one of the largest sand seas in Earth's history, formed in the arid interior of western Pangaea.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
The flora of the Early Jurassic was dominated by conifers, cycads, bennettitaleans, ginkgos, and ferns. After the upheaval of the Triassic–Jurassic extinction, which caused significant turnover in plant communities, these groups became established as the principal components of vegetation across the world.

Conifers of the extinct family Cheirolepidiaceae, which produced the distinctive pollen type known as Classopollis, were particularly abundant and well adapted to warm, dry conditions. In more humid regions, forests of araucarians, podocarps, and ginkgos grew alongside tree ferns, while horsetails and ferns thrived in wetlands and along watercourses.

Seed ferns, which had been important in the Triassic, declined significantly, and some groups became extinct. The flora of this time was well suited to the feeding habits of the growing numbers of herbivorous dinosaurs, particularly the early sauropodomorphs, which could browse the vegetation at varying heights.

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
Early Jurassic seas were home to a rich diversity of marine reptiles. Ichthyosaurs, such as the dolphin-shaped Stenopterygius, were abundant and have been found with preserved skin outlines and even embryos, showing that they gave birth to live young. Plesiosaurs such as Plesiosaurus and early pliosaurs hunted fish and cephalopods, and marine crocodylomorphs began to adapt to life in the sea.

Ammonites diversified rapidly after the Triassic–Jurassic extinction, and their fast evolution makes them valuable index fossils for dating rocks. Belemnites, bivalves, brachiopods, and crinoids were common, and modern-type corals built reefs in shallow tropical waters.

On land, early mammaliaforms such as Morganucodon and Hadrocodium were small, shrew-like animals, likely nocturnal insectivores. Pterosaurs such as Dimorphodon and Dorygnathus flew over coastal environments, and early turtles, crocodylomorphs, lizards, and amphibians occupied various niches.

sections.heading: Dinosaur Evolution
sections.body:
The Early Jurassic marked the beginning of dinosaur dominance on land. With many large crurotarsan reptiles eliminated in the Triassic–Jurassic extinction, dinosaurs rapidly diversified and increased in size, occupying most of the major ecological niches for large terrestrial vertebrates [2].

Among the predators, coelophysoids and the larger Dilophosaurus, with its distinctive twin crests, were widespread. Cryolophosaurus, discovered in Antarctica, bore an unusual crest across its head and shows that dinosaurs inhabited polar latitudes. Among the herbivores, sauropodomorphs such as Massospondylus and early true sauropods were diversifying, and some began to evolve toward the gigantic sizes of later sauropods.

Ornithischian dinosaurs also became more diverse. Early armoured forms such as Scelidosaurus and Scutellosaurus represent the ancestors of the stegosaurs and ankylosaurs, while small, bipedal heterodontosaurids had differentiated teeth, including canine-like tusks. Fossil trackways from this period, particularly in North America, provide rich evidence of dinosaur behaviour, including possible herding.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Triassic–Jurassic mass extinction was a major extinction event that occurred about 201.4 million years ago, marking the boundary between the Triassic and Jurassic periods. It is one of the 'Big Five' mass extinctions of the Phanerozoic eon, during which an estimated 70 to 80 percent of all species disappeared from the planet.

The extinction affected life both on land and in the oceans. In the seas, it eliminated the conodonts and devastated ammonoids, brachiopods, bivalves, and reef ecosystems. On land, it wiped out many groups of large reptiles that had competed with the dinosaurs, as well as most of the large amphibians.

The event is closely linked in time to the eruption of the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province, one of the largest volcanic episodes in Earth's history, which accompanied the initial rifting of Pangaea [1, 2]. By removing many competing groups, the extinction cleared the way for dinosaurs to become the dominant land animals for the remainder of the Mesozoic era.

sections.heading: Causes & Triggers
sections.body:
The primary cause of the Triassic–Jurassic extinction is thought to be the eruption of the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province (CAMP). As Pangaea began to rift apart, enormous volumes of basaltic magma erupted across a region that today spans parts of eastern North America, northwestern Africa, southwestern Europe, and northeastern South America [2]. The province originally covered an area of perhaps 10 million square kilometres.

Precise radiometric dating shows that the onset of CAMP volcanism coincided closely with the extinction [1]. The eruptions occurred in several pulses over a period of around 600,000 years [1], releasing vast amounts of carbon dioxide, sulphur dioxide, and other gases into the atmosphere. Magma intruding into sedimentary basins rich in organic material and evaporites may have released additional greenhouse gases and toxic compounds.

Alternative or contributing hypotheses have been proposed, including the release of methane from seafloor hydrates and the possibility of an asteroid impact. However, no impact crater of the right age has been convincingly identified, and the weight of evidence points to the CAMP volcanism as the principal driver of the environmental crisis.

sections.heading: Climatic/Environmental Changes
sections.body:
The gases released by CAMP volcanism triggered rapid and severe environmental changes. Carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere may have doubled or more, driving intense global warming. Evidence from fossil leaves, whose density of stomata (breathing pores) is related to atmospheric carbon dioxide, indicates a sharp rise in carbon dioxide across the boundary [3].

The increase in carbon dioxide also caused ocean acidification, making it more difficult for marine organisms to build shells and skeletons from calcium carbonate. This is reflected in a so-called 'calcification crisis', in which reef-building organisms and many shelled invertebrates suffered severe losses [4]. Pulses of sulphur dioxide may also have caused short episodes of cooling and acid rain.

The warming of the oceans reduced their capacity to hold dissolved oxygen, contributing to the spread of anoxic and euxinic waters in some regions. On land, sharp swings in temperature and rainfall disrupted plant communities, as shown by changes in fossil pollen and spores, including a prominent fern spike in some regions.

sections.heading: Biological Impact
sections.body:
In the oceans, the extinction was particularly severe. Conodonts, eel-like animals whose tooth-like fossils are abundant in Paleozoic and Triassic rocks, disappeared completely. Ammonoids suffered catastrophic losses, with only a single lineage surviving to give rise to the ammonites of the Jurassic and Cretaceous. Brachiopods, bivalves, gastropods, and marine reptiles such as the placodonts were also heavily affected, and reef ecosystems collapsed.

On land, the extinction removed many groups of archosaurs and other reptiles. The crurotarsans, including the phytosaurs, aetosaurs, and large predatory rauisuchians, which had been dominant in many Triassic ecosystems, were largely eliminated, leaving only the ancestors of crocodiles. Most large amphibians, such as the temnospondyls, were also lost, as were many synapsid groups.

The dinosaurs, pterosaurs, crocodylomorphs, early mammals, turtles, and lizard relatives survived the extinction. The reasons for the survival of the dinosaurs are debated, but they may have been aided by their efficient respiratory systems, high metabolic rates, or ability to tolerate a range of environmental conditions.

sections.heading: Legacy
sections.body:
The Triassic–Jurassic extinction was a pivotal moment in the history of life. By eliminating the crurotarsans and other competitors, it allowed the dinosaurs to rise to dominance on land during the Jurassic, beginning an era of dinosaur supremacy that would last for more than 135 million years until the K-Pg extinction.

In the oceans, the survivors of the extinction diversified rapidly during the Early Jurassic. Ammonites radiated into hundreds of new species, and the recovery of reef ecosystems saw the rise of modern types of corals. Marine reptiles such as ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs flourished, and new groups of marine animals took advantage of the vacated ecological space.

The extinction also had a lasting geological legacy. The CAMP volcanism was linked to the break-up of Pangaea and the opening of the central Atlantic Ocean, reshaping the geography of the planet. Today, the event serves as an important case study for understanding how rapid carbon release, global warming, and ocean acidification can affect life on Earth.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Late Triassic was the final epoch of the Triassic period, lasting from about 237 to 201.4 million years ago [1]. At more than 35 million years in duration, it was the longest epoch of the Triassic and a time of profound evolutionary change, during which many of the major groups of modern vertebrates first appeared.

During this epoch, the first dinosaurs, pterosaurs, crocodylomorphs, turtles, and mammaliaforms evolved, alongside a wide variety of other reptiles that later went extinct. The supercontinent Pangaea was fully assembled, although signs of its impending break-up were becoming apparent.

The Late Triassic was punctuated by the Carnian Pluvial Episode, a period of increased rainfall and climatic change that reshaped ecosystems, and ended with the Triassic–Jurassic mass extinction, one of the five largest extinctions in Earth's history.

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
The climate of the Late Triassic was generally hot, with no evidence of polar ice. The immense size of Pangaea created strong seasonal contrasts, with a pronounced monsoonal climate: intense summer rains alternated with long dry seasons. The interior of the supercontinent was largely arid, and extensive deserts and salt flats developed in some regions.

Around 234 to 232 million years ago, the Carnian Pluvial Episode brought a dramatic shift to a wetter climate across much of the world. Linked to volcanic eruptions of the Wrangellia large igneous province, this episode was marked by global warming, increased rainfall, and changes in ocean chemistry [2]. It coincided with extinctions among some groups and the diversification of others, including dinosaurs and modern-type conifers [2].

Following the Carnian Pluvial Episode, the climate returned to drier conditions for much of the remaining Late Triassic. Atmospheric carbon dioxide levels were considerably higher than today, and temperatures were warm across all latitudes.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
In the Late Triassic, the continents were united into the supercontinent Pangaea, which stretched from the North Pole to the South Pole and was surrounded by the global ocean Panthalassa. The Tethys Ocean formed a large, wedge-shaped embayment on the eastern side of Pangaea, extending westward between the northern and southern parts of the supercontinent.

Rifting was beginning to pull Pangaea apart. A series of rift basins developed along the future margins of the Atlantic Ocean, from eastern North America to northwestern Africa and Europe. These basins filled with lake and river sediments, preserving fossils of fish, reptiles, and footprints, such as those found in the Newark Supergroup of eastern North America.

Much of central Europe was covered by shallow basins that alternated between marine and continental conditions, forming the characteristic three-part Germanic Triassic succession. In the Tethys, extensive carbonate platforms and reefs developed, forming the rocks that now make up the Dolomites of northern Italy.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
Late Triassic vegetation was dominated by gymnosperms, including conifers, cycads, bennettitaleans, ginkgos, and seed ferns. Conifers became increasingly important after the Carnian Pluvial Episode, with the rise of groups ancestral to modern araucarians and other families.

In the Southern Hemisphere, the seed fern Dicroidium formed extensive forests and was one of the most characteristic plants of the Triassic in Gondwana. In the Northern Hemisphere, conifers and cycad-like plants were more prominent. The famous Petrified Forest of Arizona preserves large logs of the conifer Agathoxylon, which grew in forests along rivers in a tropical, monsoonal climate.

Ferns, horsetails, and other spore-bearing plants thrived in wetter environments, and the first modern families of ferns appeared during this time. The diversification of plants provided an important food source for the growing variety of herbivorous reptiles, including the early sauropodomorph dinosaurs.

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
Late Triassic ecosystems were remarkably diverse. On land, a wide variety of archosaurs dominated. The crurotarsans — relatives of crocodiles — included the armoured, herbivorous aetosaurs, the crocodile-like phytosaurs, and the large predatory rauisuchians, which were apex predators in many ecosystems. The first crocodylomorphs were small, lightly built, and long-legged.

Other reptiles included the beaked rhynchosaurs and the sprawling, parrot-beaked dicynodonts, the last of the great synapsid herbivores. The first turtles, such as Proganochelys, appeared with fully formed shells, and large amphibians such as metoposaurs lived in rivers and lakes. The earliest mammaliaforms, small shrew-like animals, evolved from cynodont ancestors near the end of the epoch.

In the seas, ichthyosaurs reached enormous sizes; Shonisaurus and related forms may have exceeded 20 metres in length. Placodonts and nothosaurs lived in shallow coastal waters, and ammonoids, bivalves, and corals were abundant. The first pterosaurs took to the skies, becoming the first vertebrates to achieve powered flight.

sections.heading: Dinosaur Evolution
sections.body:
The earliest known dinosaurs appeared in the early Late Triassic, around 233 to 230 million years ago. Fossils from the Ischigualasto Formation of Argentina and the Santa Maria Formation of Brazil, including Eoraptor, Herrerasaurus, and Staurikosaurus, represent some of the oldest known dinosaurs [3]. These early forms were relatively small, bipedal animals.

During the Late Triassic, dinosaurs diversified into their three major lineages: the theropods, the sauropodomorphs, and the ornithischians [3]. Early theropods such as Coelophysis were lightly built, agile predators, and fossils from Ghost Ranch in New Mexico preserve hundreds of individuals. Sauropodomorphs such as Plateosaurus became the first large herbivorous dinosaurs, reaching lengths of up to 10 metres.

Despite this diversification, dinosaurs were not yet the dominant land animals for much of the Late Triassic. The crurotarsan archosaurs remained ecologically important, and it was only after the Triassic–Jurassic extinction removed many of these competitors that the dinosaurs rose to dominance [4].

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Middle Triassic was the second epoch of the Triassic period, lasting from about 247 to 237 million years ago [1]. It was a time of recovery and renewal following the catastrophic Permian–Triassic extinction, which had wiped out most life on Earth roughly 5 to 10 million years earlier.

By the Middle Triassic, ecosystems on land and in the sea had largely recovered their complexity. New groups of animals, including the archosaurs, marine reptiles, and the ancestors of mammals, diversified rapidly and filled the ecological niches left vacant by the extinction [2].

The epoch is known for exceptional fossil sites, such as Monte San Giorgio on the border of Switzerland and Italy, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, which preserves a remarkable variety of marine reptiles and fish in extraordinary detail.

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
The climate of the Middle Triassic was generally warm and dry, although less extreme than the hot conditions of the Early Triassic. There was no permanent ice at the poles, and global temperatures remained considerably higher than today. Atmospheric carbon dioxide levels were high, although lower than at the peak of the Early Triassic greenhouse.

The vast size of Pangaea produced a strongly seasonal climate, with a powerful monsoon circulation. Coastal regions and areas near the Tethys Ocean received seasonal rainfall, while the interior of the supercontinent was dominated by arid and semi-arid conditions, with extensive red beds and evaporite deposits.

The gradual stabilisation of the climate during the Middle Triassic, following the extreme warmth and environmental instability of the Early Triassic, is thought to have contributed to the recovery of life, allowing complex ecosystems to re-establish on land and in the oceans [2].

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
During the Middle Triassic, the supercontinent Pangaea was fully assembled, stretching from pole to pole and forming a giant 'C' shape around the Tethys Ocean. The vast global ocean Panthalassa surrounded the supercontinent, covering most of the planet's surface.

The margins of the Tethys Ocean were home to extensive shallow seas and carbonate platforms. In what is now Europe, the Germanic Basin was periodically flooded by the sea, depositing the Muschelkalk limestones, which are rich in marine fossils. Meanwhile, in the southern Alps, carbonate platforms and deep basins developed, forming the rocks that now make up parts of the Dolomites.

In the interior of Pangaea, large regions were covered by rivers, floodplains, and lakes, as well as deserts. In the Southern Hemisphere, the basins of Gondwana, such as the Karoo Basin of South Africa, accumulated thick sequences of continental sediments, preserving important fossils of synapsids and early archosaurs.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
Following the devastation of the Permian–Triassic extinction, plant communities recovered during the Middle Triassic. Forests of gymnosperms, including conifers, cycads, and ginkgos, re-established themselves across much of the world, replacing the lycopsid-dominated vegetation that had characterised the Early Triassic in many regions.

In Gondwana, the seed fern Dicroidium became dominant, forming extensive woodlands. In the Northern Hemisphere, conifers such as Voltzia and early members of modern conifer families were common, alongside horsetails, ferns, and seed ferns.

The recovery of plant communities provided a foundation for the diversification of herbivorous animals on land, including the dicynodonts, rhynchosaurs, and early archosaurs. The re-establishment of forests also helped to stabilise soils and reduce erosion, which had been extreme in the immediate aftermath of the Permian–Triassic extinction.

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
In the seas, the Middle Triassic saw a remarkable diversification of marine reptiles. Nothosaurs, with their long necks and sharp teeth, hunted fish in shallow coastal waters, while placodonts, with their broad, flat teeth, crushed shellfish on the seafloor. Ichthyosaurs, which had first appeared in the Early Triassic, grew larger and more diverse, and the bizarre, long-necked Tanystropheus hunted along the shoreline.

Marine invertebrates also recovered, with ammonoids, bivalves, and crinoids becoming abundant. The first scleractinian corals — the group that includes modern reef-building corals — appeared during this epoch, beginning the gradual reconstruction of reef ecosystems [3].

On land, the dicynodonts and cynodonts, groups of synapsids related to the ancestors of mammals, were important herbivores and predators. Rhynchosaurs were common in many regions, and large temnospondyl amphibians such as Mastodonsaurus lived in rivers and lakes. Early archosaurs, including crurotarsans and the ancestors of dinosaurs and pterosaurs, were diversifying.

sections.heading: Reptilian Evolution
sections.body:
The Middle Triassic was a crucial period in the evolution of reptiles, particularly the archosaurs. The archosaurs split into two major lineages: the pseudosuchians, which include crocodiles and their relatives, and the avemetatarsalians, which include dinosaurs, pterosaurs, and birds.

The pseudosuchians diversified rapidly, producing a range of forms, including large predatory rauisuchians such as Ticinosuchus and early aetosaurs. On the avemetatarsalian side, early relatives of dinosaurs, known as dinosauromorphs, appeared. Small, lightly built animals such as Lagerpeton and Marasuchus, together with the silesaurids, show many of the features that would later characterise dinosaurs.

The possible earliest dinosaur, Nyasasaurus from Tanzania, is dated to the late Middle Triassic, around 243 million years ago, although its status as a true dinosaur remains debated [4]. In the oceans, the sauropterygians — the group that includes nothosaurs, placodonts, and the ancestors of the plesiosaurs — underwent an extensive radiation.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Early Triassic was the first epoch of the Triassic period and of the Mesozoic era, lasting from about 251.9 to 247 million years ago. It began immediately after the Permian–Triassic extinction, often known as the 'Great Dying', the most severe mass extinction in Earth's history, which eliminated around 90 percent of marine species and about 70 percent of terrestrial vertebrate species.

The Early Triassic was a time of harsh environmental conditions and slow biological recovery. Ecosystems were impoverished and dominated by a small number of hardy 'disaster taxa' that thrived in the absence of competition [1].

Despite these challenges, the Early Triassic was also a time of evolutionary innovation. Many groups that would later dominate the Mesozoic, including the archosaurs and the marine reptiles, first appeared or began to diversify during this epoch.

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
The climate of the Early Triassic was extremely hot. Following the massive eruptions of the Siberian Traps, which are thought to have caused the Permian–Triassic extinction, atmospheric carbon dioxide levels were very high, and global temperatures rose dramatically. Sea surface temperatures in the tropics may have reached 40 °C or more, making large areas of the equatorial ocean and land nearly uninhabitable [2].

This extreme heat led to a phenomenon known as the 'equatorial tetrapod gap', in which fossils of land vertebrates are very rare in low latitudes, suggesting that many animals were forced to live at higher latitudes where temperatures were more tolerable [2].

The Early Triassic climate was also marked by repeated environmental upheavals, including fluctuations in the carbon cycle, episodes of ocean anoxia, and ocean acidification. A particularly severe crisis, the Smithian–Spathian event, occurred around 249 million years ago and caused further extinctions among ammonoids and conodonts [1, 2].

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
During the Early Triassic, all the continents were joined together in the supercontinent Pangaea, which stretched from the North Pole to the South Pole. The global ocean Panthalassa surrounded the supercontinent, while the Tethys Ocean formed a large embayment on its eastern side.

The interior of Pangaea was largely dry, with extensive deserts and red beds. In many regions, the loss of vegetation following the extinction led to a change in river systems, from meandering rivers with stable banks to braided rivers with rapidly shifting channels, reflecting increased erosion and runoff.

The Siberian Traps, a vast volcanic province in what is now Siberia, continued to erupt into the earliest Triassic, covering an area of millions of square kilometres with basalt. The ocean was stratified, and large areas of the seafloor were starved of oxygen, preventing the recovery of marine life in many regions.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
The Permian–Triassic extinction had a devastating effect on plant life. The Glossopteris flora, which had dominated the southern continents during the Permian, disappeared, and coal formation ceased globally for several million years, a phenomenon known as the 'coal gap'.

In the aftermath of the extinction, vegetation was dominated by hardy, opportunistic plants. The small lycopsid Pleuromeia, a relative of modern quillworts, was particularly widespread and formed low-growing communities along coastlines. Spore-bearing plants such as ferns and lycopsids were common, and fungal spores are abundant in some sediments from around the extinction.

Forests slowly began to recover during the Early Triassic, with the gradual re-establishment of conifers and seed ferns. By the end of the epoch, more diverse plant communities were beginning to appear, laying the foundations for the recovery of terrestrial ecosystems in the Middle Triassic.

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
The fauna of the Early Triassic was dominated by a small number of survivor species. On land, the dicynodont Lystrosaurus, a pig-sized herbivore with a beak and two tusks, was extraordinarily abundant, making up the vast majority of vertebrate fossils in some regions. Its fossils have been found in Antarctica, Africa, India, and China, providing important evidence for the existence of Pangaea.

Other land animals included small cynodonts such as Thrinaxodon, which may have lived in burrows to escape the heat, and a variety of early archosauromorphs, including Proterosuchus. Temnospondyl amphibians were common in freshwater environments.

In the oceans, marine life was slow to recover. The seafloor was dominated by a few species of bivalves, such as Claraia, and microbial mats and stromatolites became common again, reflecting the lack of grazing animals. Ammonoids and conodonts diversified rapidly but suffered repeated setbacks. Remarkably, the first marine reptiles, including early ichthyosauromorphs such as Cartorhynchus, appeared within a few million years of the extinction [3].

sections.heading: Reptilian Evolution
sections.body:
The Early Triassic was a critical period for reptilian evolution. In the aftermath of the Permian–Triassic extinction, the archosauromorphs — a group that includes the archosaurs and their close relatives — underwent a rapid radiation, producing a variety of forms, from small insectivores to large predators such as Erythrosuchus, which reached lengths of up to 5 metres.

The archosaurs proper, the group that would later give rise to crocodiles, dinosaurs, pterosaurs, and birds, originated during the Early Triassic or perhaps in the latest Permian. Fossil footprints from Poland suggest that dinosauromorphs, the close relatives of dinosaurs, may have existed as early as 250 million years ago [4].

The Early Triassic also saw the rapid evolution of marine reptiles from terrestrial ancestors. The ichthyosauromorphs, sauropterygians, and other groups colonised the oceans, taking advantage of the ecological opportunities created by the extinction. This rapid radiation of reptiles on land and in the sea set the stage for the Age of Reptiles that would characterise the rest of the Mesozoic era.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Permian–Triassic (P–T) mass extinction, often called the 'Great Dying', was the most severe biological crisis in the history of complex life. It took place about 251.9 million years ago, marking the end of the Permian period and of the Paleozoic era, and the beginning of the Triassic and the Mesozoic. An estimated 80 to 90 per cent of marine species and around 70 per cent of terrestrial vertebrate species disappeared.

High-precision uranium–lead dating of volcanic ash beds in South China, especially at the Meishan section that defines the boundary, shows that the main pulse of extinction was geologically abrupt, unfolding over perhaps 60,000 years or less [1]. In the rock record the event appears as a sharp loss of fossils, a dramatic negative swing in carbon isotopes, and a shift to sediments that record oxygen-starved, acidic, and overheated seas.

The P–T extinction is the largest of the 'Big Five' mass extinctions. It reset the course of evolution, ending the long reign of Paleozoic marine faunas and of the synapsid-dominated land ecosystems, and setting the stage for the Mesozoic world of dinosaurs, marine reptiles, and modern-style reef and seafloor communities.

sections.heading: Causes & Triggers
sections.body:
The principal trigger is now widely accepted to be the eruption of the Siberian Traps, one of the largest volcanic provinces in Earth's history. Over a few hundred thousand years, several million cubic kilometres of basaltic lava and pyroclastic material erupted across what is now northern Russia, releasing vast quantities of carbon dioxide, sulphur dioxide, and halogens into the atmosphere.

Crucially, much of the magma did not simply reach the surface but intruded as sills into thick sedimentary basins rich in coal, oil shale, evaporites, and carbonates. Heating these rocks released enormous additional volumes of carbon dioxide and methane, as well as chlorinated and brominated gases capable of damaging the ozone layer [2]. Coal fly ash found in Canadian Arctic sediments of boundary age is thought to record this combustion of coal by intruding magma.

The timing of the main intrusive phase of the Siberian Traps matches the extinction horizon closely, strengthening the causal link [2]. Other proposed contributors, such as a bolide impact or a sudden release of methane hydrates from the seafloor, lack convincing evidence as primary causes, though methane release may have amplified the carbon-cycle disturbance once warming began.

sections.heading: Climatic/Environmental Changes
sections.body:
The injection of greenhouse gases drove extreme global warming. Oxygen isotopes from conodont fossils suggest that tropical sea-surface temperatures rose by around 8 to 10 °C, reaching perhaps 35 to 40 °C in the earliest Triassic — hotter than most marine animals can tolerate [3]. On land, equatorial regions became so hot that they may have been largely uninhabitable for vertebrates for millions of years [3].

The oceans suffered a cascade of linked stresses. Warmer water holds less oxygen, and weakened ocean circulation allowed anoxic and even euxinic (hydrogen sulphide-rich) waters to spread across continental shelves. At the same time, rapid uptake of carbon dioxide caused ocean acidification, which particularly harmed organisms that built heavily calcified skeletons. Evidence for these conditions includes widespread black shales, pyrite framboids, and biomarkers of green sulphur bacteria.

On land, acid rain, ozone depletion, and wildfire contributed to the collapse of forests. Plant spore assemblages show malformed grains consistent with increased ultraviolet radiation, and a widespread 'coal gap' in the Early Triassic indicates that peat-forming forests vanished for millions of years. Soil erosion increased sharply as vegetation was lost, and river systems shifted from meandering to braided forms.

sections.heading: Biological Impact
sections.body:
Marine life was devastated. The tabulate and rugose corals, the last trilobites, and the blastoid echinoderms were wiped out entirely. Brachiopods, crinoids, bryozoans, ammonoids, and fusulinid foraminifera were reduced to a handful of surviving lineages. Animals with heavy calcium carbonate skeletons and limited control over their internal chemistry suffered disproportionately, consistent with the combined effects of warming, anoxia, and acidification.

On land, the diverse communities of synapsids that had dominated the late Permian — including gorgonopsians and many dicynodont groups — largely disappeared. It is also the only mass extinction known to have caused major losses among insects. Survivors included the hardy dicynodont Lystrosaurus, which became extraordinarily abundant across Pangaea in the earliest Triassic, a classic example of a 'disaster taxon'.

Recovery was unusually slow. Early Triassic ecosystems were species-poor and dominated by a few opportunistic groups, and microbial mats and stromatolites temporarily returned to prominence in shallow seas. Repeated environmental perturbations through the Early Triassic delayed full ecological recovery for perhaps 5 to 10 million years, and complex reef ecosystems did not reappear until the Middle Triassic [4].

sections.heading: Legacy
sections.body:
The Great Dying fundamentally reshaped the trajectory of life. In the seas, the brachiopod- and crinoid-dominated 'Paleozoic fauna' gave way to the 'Modern fauna' dominated by bivalves, gastropods, crustaceans, and bony fishes. New groups such as scleractinian corals, modern sea urchins, and ichthyosaurs emerged during the recovery, establishing the foundations of marine ecosystems that persist today.

On land, the extinction cleared space for the archosaurs, the group that would give rise to crocodilians, pterosaurs, and dinosaurs, while the surviving cynodonts eventually gave rise to the first mammals. The Mesozoic world of reptilian dominance can therefore be traced directly to the opportunities created by this catastrophe.

The P–T extinction is also of great interest as a natural analogue for modern climate change. It demonstrates how rapid carbon release can drive warming, ocean deoxygenation, and acidification simultaneously, and how these stresses can combine to cause biological collapse. Although the rate and scale of carbon emissions differed, the event offers a sobering illustration of the consequences of severe disruption to Earth's carbon cycle.
