sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Carboniferous Rainforest Collapse (CRC) was a major ecological upheaval that struck the vast tropical coal forests of Euramerica around 305 million years ago, near the boundary between the Moscovian and Kasimovian stages of the Late Pennsylvanian. The sprawling, humid wetland forests that had covered much of the equatorial lowlands fragmented into isolated 'islands' of forest separated by drier landscapes [1].

Unlike the 'Big Five' mass extinctions, the CRC was not a catastrophe concentrated in the oceans, nor did it eliminate an overwhelming fraction of all species. Its effects were felt chiefly in terrestrial ecosystems, particularly among the plants that formed the coal swamps and the animals that depended on them. The collapse is recorded in coal-bearing sequences across North America and Europe, where the dominant vegetation changes markedly and coal formation diminishes [2].

The event is significant because it represents one of the first major restructurings of land ecosystems driven by climate change. It marks a transition from the iconic lycopsid-dominated coal swamps of the Carboniferous to drier, seasonal environments that would characterise much of the Permian.

sections.heading: Causes & Triggers
sections.body:
The CRC was driven primarily by climatic shifts associated with the Late Paleozoic Ice Age. During the Carboniferous, large ice sheets waxed and waned over the southern supercontinent of Gondwana, and the growth and retreat of these ice sheets drove cycles of sea-level change and alternating wet and dry phases in the tropics. Around 305 million years ago, these fluctuations intensified, pushing the equatorial climate towards greater aridity [3].

The assembly of Pangaea also played a role. As continents merged, large interior regions became more distant from oceanic moisture sources, and mountain ranges such as the Central Pangean Mountains altered atmospheric circulation. These changes strengthened seasonality and reduced the reliability of rainfall that the wetland forests required.

Some researchers have also suggested that changes in atmospheric carbon dioxide played a part. The burial of enormous amounts of organic carbon in coal swamps had drawn down atmospheric carbon dioxide over millions of years, contributing to glaciation [2, 3]. Fluctuations in carbon dioxide levels, possibly influenced by volcanic activity, may have pushed the climate across thresholds that destabilised the forest ecosystems.

sections.heading: Climatic/Environmental Changes
sections.body:
The key environmental change was a shift from consistently humid, everwet tropical conditions to a more seasonally dry climate. Wetland habitats contracted as water tables fell and rainfall became less predictable. Areas that had supported dense peat-forming swamps became drier floodplains, and the extent of coal deposition declined markedly in many basins.

The collapse appears to have occurred in stages rather than as a single event. Repeated glacial–interglacial cycles caused episodes of drying followed by partial recovery, gradually eroding the resilience of the wetland ecosystems. Each drier interval allowed seasonally adapted plants to gain ground, while the wetland flora retreated into smaller and more isolated refuges.

The resulting landscape was a patchwork: remnant wetland forests persisted in favourable lowland settings, surrounded by more open vegetation adapted to drier conditions. This fragmentation had important consequences for the animals living in these habitats, as populations became isolated and the area of suitable habitat shrank.

sections.heading: Biological Impact
sections.body:
Among plants, the giant arborescent lycopsids such as Lepidodendron and Sigillaria, which had dominated the coal swamps, declined dramatically in Euramerica. Tree ferns, which were better suited to disturbed and drier conditions, became increasingly prominent, and seed plants such as conifers and cordaitaleans expanded in drier habitats. Overall plant diversity was not drastically reduced, but the composition of the flora changed fundamentally [2].

Among animals, the effects were most pronounced for amphibians and other tetrapods closely tied to wetland environments. Studies of tetrapod fossil assemblages suggest that diversity declined after the collapse and that the surviving communities became more endemic, with each forest fragment hosting its own distinct fauna, as predicted by island biogeography theory [1]. Large arthropods of the coal forests, such as the giant millipede-like Arthropleura, also declined.

Amniotes — the early reptiles and synapsids, which laid eggs with protective membranes and were less dependent on water for reproduction — appear to have fared comparatively well. Their ability to exploit drier habitats and to diversify their diets, including the early adoption of herbivory, allowed them to expand into the newly available environments [1].

sections.heading: Legacy
sections.body:
The CRC helped shift the balance of terrestrial life from amphibians towards amniotes. In the drier world of the latest Carboniferous and Permian, reptiles and synapsids diversified rapidly, laying the foundations for the synapsid-dominated ecosystems of the Permian and, ultimately, for the lineages leading to both mammals and dinosaurs.

The event also marked a turning point in plant evolution. Seed plants, better adapted to seasonal drought, began their rise to dominance, while the spore-bearing lycopsid trees never regained their former prominence in the Northern Hemisphere. The decline of the vast coal swamps also reduced the rate at which organic carbon was buried, influencing the long-term carbon cycle and atmospheric composition.

The CRC provides a valuable case study in how climate change and habitat fragmentation can reshape ecosystems without necessarily causing a mass extinction. Its pattern of habitat loss, isolation, and community turnover offers insights relevant to the modern world, where tropical forests are being fragmented by human activity and climate change.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Late Devonian mass extinction was a prolonged series of biological crises that unfolded over the final 10 to 15 million years of the Devonian period. Rather than a single catastrophe, it comprised several pulses, the two most severe being the Kellwasser event at the Frasnian–Famennian boundary about 372 million years ago and the Hangenberg event at the Devonian–Carboniferous boundary about 359 million years ago [1].

Together these crises eliminated an estimated 70 to 75 per cent of marine species. The Kellwasser event is named after the Kellwasser valley in Germany, where two distinctive dark, organic-rich limestone horizons record episodes of oxygen-poor seas. The Hangenberg event is likewise marked by a widespread black shale, followed by sandstones that indicate a sharp fall in sea level.

The Late Devonian extinction is counted among the 'Big Five' mass extinctions. It is notable for having struck tropical reef ecosystems particularly hard and for occurring at a time when life on land, including the first forests and the earliest four-limbed vertebrates, was undergoing profound evolutionary change.

sections.heading: Causes & Triggers
sections.body:
The causes of the Late Devonian crises remain debated, and several mechanisms likely interacted. One leading hypothesis links the extinctions to the spread of land plants. During the Middle and Late Devonian, the first true trees, such as Archaeopteris, formed extensive forests with deep root systems. These accelerated the chemical weathering of rocks and the formation of soils, washing large amounts of nutrients into rivers and coastal seas [2].

This nutrient influx is thought to have fuelled algal blooms in shallow seas, whose decay consumed dissolved oxygen and produced widespread anoxia, recorded by the black shales of the Kellwasser and Hangenberg horizons. Enhanced weathering and burial of organic carbon would also have drawn down atmospheric carbon dioxide, contributing to global cooling [2].

Volcanism has also been implicated. Large igneous provinces such as the Viluy Traps in Siberia and magmatism in the Pripyat–Dnieper–Donets rift erupted around the time of the Frasnian–Famennian boundary, and mercury anomalies in boundary sediments support a volcanic contribution [3]. Asteroid impacts, such as the Alamo and Siljan structures, have been proposed but are not considered primary causes [3]. For the Hangenberg event, evidence of increased ultraviolet damage in plant spores has suggested ozone depletion as an additional stress [1].

sections.heading: Climatic/Environmental Changes
sections.body:
The Late Devonian was marked by repeated swings in climate and ocean chemistry. Oxygen isotope evidence suggests that the Kellwasser horizons coincided with episodes of rapid temperature change, with both warming and cooling phases recorded. Large positive carbon isotope excursions in the same intervals reflect massive burial of organic matter in oxygen-starved seafloor sediments.

Toward the end of the Devonian, the climate cooled significantly. Glacial deposits of latest Devonian age are found in South America, particularly in Brazil and Bolivia, indicating that ice sheets grew on Gondwana. This glaciation lowered sea levels around the time of the Hangenberg event, exposing continental shelves and destroying shallow marine habitats [1].

The combination of anoxia, temperature fluctuations, and sea-level change placed severe stress on shallow-water ecosystems, especially in the tropics. Warm-water organisms, adapted to stable conditions, were particularly vulnerable to cooling, while the spread of anoxic waters onto the continental shelves eliminated habitats for bottom-dwelling animals.

sections.heading: Biological Impact
sections.body:
The most dramatic casualty of the Kellwasser event was the great reef ecosystem of the Devonian. Built largely by stromatoporoid sponges and tabulate and rugose corals, Middle Devonian reefs were among the most extensive in Earth's history. After the Frasnian–Famennian crisis, these metazoan reefs collapsed and did not recover to a comparable scale for many millions of years. Brachiopods, trilobites, ammonoids, and conodonts also suffered heavy losses.

Vertebrates were strongly affected as well. The armoured placoderm fishes, which had been the dominant vertebrates of Devonian seas, declined through the Late Devonian and vanished entirely at the Hangenberg event [1]. Many lineages of jawless fishes and lobe-finned fishes also disappeared, and the early tetrapods suffered substantial losses.

The extinction is notable for being driven as much by a lack of new species arising as by the loss of existing ones. Studies of origination rates suggest that speciation slowed dramatically during the Late Devonian, perhaps because invasive species spread widely as sea levels changed, reducing the regional isolation that normally encourages new species to form [4].

sections.heading: Legacy
sections.body:
The Late Devonian crises reshaped vertebrate evolution. With the placoderms gone, cartilaginous fishes such as sharks and ray-finned fishes diversified in the Carboniferous, establishing the basic structure of fish communities that persists today. The survivors among the early tetrapods gave rise to the lineages that would conquer the land during the Carboniferous.

The collapse of the Devonian reefs had a long-lasting effect on marine ecosystems. Reef building in the Early Carboniferous was dominated by microbial and mud-mound structures rather than large coral frameworks, and it took a long time for complex reef communities to re-establish themselves.

The Late Devonian extinction also highlights the deep connections between life on land and in the sea. The hypothesis that the evolution of forests helped trigger marine anoxia illustrates how biological innovations can transform global biogeochemical cycles, with consequences for the entire biosphere [2]. It remains an important example of how gradual environmental change, punctuated by sharper crises, can produce a mass extinction.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The end-Ordovician mass extinction, also known as the Late Ordovician or Ordovician–Silurian extinction, was the first of the 'Big Five' mass extinctions and the second most severe in terms of the proportion of species lost. It took place between about 445 and 443 million years ago, during the Hirnantian stage at the very end of the Ordovician period, and eliminated an estimated 85 per cent of marine species [1].

The extinction occurred in two main pulses. The first coincided with the onset of a major glaciation, and the second came at the end of the glacial episode, when the ice melted and climate warmed again. Each pulse struck different groups of organisms, reflecting the very different environmental stresses involved [1, 2].

Because almost all animal life at the time lived in the oceans, the end-Ordovician extinction was essentially a marine crisis. It brought an abrupt end to the extraordinary diversification of the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event, although the overall ecological structure of marine communities survived relatively intact compared with later mass extinctions.

sections.heading: Causes & Triggers
sections.body:
The primary driver of the extinction was a short but intense glaciation centred on the supercontinent Gondwana, which lay over the South Pole in what is now North Africa and South America. Glacial deposits of Hirnantian age, including striated pavements and tillites, are preserved across the Sahara, recording ice sheets that spread over vast areas [3].

Why this glaciation occurred during a time of generally warm greenhouse climate remains debated. One hypothesis is that the weathering of newly uplifted mountains formed during the Taconic orogeny drew down atmospheric carbon dioxide. Another proposes that the spread of early non-vascular land plants, such as mosses and liverworts, enhanced chemical weathering and further reduced carbon dioxide levels. Increased burial of organic carbon in the oceans may also have played a role [2].

Other possible contributors have been suggested, including volcanic activity, recorded by mercury anomalies in some sections, and toxic metal enrichment in the oceans. A more speculative hypothesis proposes that a gamma-ray burst from a nearby star stripped away part of the ozone layer, though there is no direct evidence for this [4].

sections.heading: Climatic/Environmental Changes
sections.body:
The Hirnantian glaciation caused global cooling, with tropical sea-surface temperatures falling by several degrees. Oxygen isotope data from brachiopod shells and conodonts indicate a significant temperature drop and growth of ice volume [3]. A large positive carbon isotope excursion, known as the Hirnantian isotope carbon excursion (HICE), records major disruption to the carbon cycle during this interval.

The growth of ice sheets locked up enormous volumes of water, causing sea level to fall by perhaps 50 to 100 metres. The shallow epicontinental seas that had flooded the continents during the Ordovician drained away, destroying vast areas of habitat for marine organisms [1]. Ocean circulation also changed, with cold, oxygenated deep waters becoming more prevalent.

When the glaciation ended, rapid warming and sea-level rise brought a new set of stresses. Oxygen-poor waters spread across the continental shelves, recorded by widespread black shales at the base of the Silurian. Organisms that had adapted to cold, well-oxygenated conditions during the glacial interval were then devastated by the return of warm, anoxic waters [2].

sections.heading: Biological Impact
sections.body:
The first pulse of extinction, at the start of the glaciation, struck organisms adapted to warm, shallow tropical seas. Brachiopods, bryozoans, trilobites, conodonts, and graptolites all suffered heavy losses. Planktonic and free-swimming species were particularly hard hit, as were species with restricted geographical ranges in the shrinking shallow seas.

The second pulse, at the end of the glaciation, eliminated many of the cold-adapted species that had flourished during the glacial interval, such as the brachiopods of the Hirnantia fauna, which had spread widely during the cold phase. Deep-water organisms were also affected by the spread of anoxic waters.

Despite the high proportion of species lost, the ecological impact of the extinction was relatively modest compared with later crises. The overall structure of marine communities, dominated by brachiopods, crinoids, and corals, remained broadly similar after the extinction. Recovery was also relatively rapid, with diversity rebounding within a few million years during the early Silurian [1].

sections.heading: Legacy
sections.body:
The end-Ordovician extinction pruned many of the lineages that had arisen during the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event, but the survivors went on to establish the marine communities of the Silurian and Devonian. Graptolites, although severely reduced, recovered and diversified again in the Silurian, while reef ecosystems built by corals and stromatoporoids expanded in the warmer seas that followed.

The extinction also coincided with important developments on land. Early land plants continued to spread during the Silurian, and the first vascular plants appeared shortly afterwards. The changes in climate and ocean chemistry at the end of the Ordovician helped set the scene for these developments.

The end-Ordovician extinction is unusual among the 'Big Five' in being linked primarily to global cooling and glaciation rather than warming. It demonstrates that rapid climate change in either direction can be devastating for life, especially when it alters sea level and ocean chemistry on a global scale.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event (GOBE) was a prolonged evolutionary radiation during which the diversity of marine life increased dramatically. Spanning much of the Ordovician period, from about 485 to 445 million years ago, with its most intense phase around 470 million years ago in the Middle Ordovician, it saw the number of marine genera roughly triple and the number of families increase several-fold [1].

Whereas the Cambrian explosion produced most of the major animal body plans, the GOBE filled the oceans with a vast variety of species within those groups. It was a diversification at lower taxonomic levels — genera, families, and orders — and it established the ecological structure of marine communities that would persist for much of the rest of the Paleozoic era.

The GOBE is regarded as one of the most important evolutionary events in the history of life. It created the so-called 'Paleozoic evolutionary fauna', dominated by brachiopods, crinoids, bryozoans, corals, and cephalopods, which replaced the trilobite-dominated 'Cambrian fauna' as the principal component of marine ecosystems [1].

sections.heading: Causes & Triggers
sections.body:
The causes of the GOBE are thought to involve a combination of geological, climatic, and biological factors. During the Ordovician, the continents were widely dispersed, and high sea levels flooded the continental interiors with extensive shallow seas. This geographical configuration created many isolated habitats and provinces, promoting the formation of new species.

Climate change also played an important role. Oxygen isotope evidence from conodonts suggests that the extremely hot conditions of the Early Ordovician gave way to progressive cooling, bringing tropical sea temperatures down to levels similar to those of today by the Middle Ordovician [2]. This cooling may have made the oceans more hospitable for many organisms and increased the oxygen content of seawater.

Other proposed triggers include rising atmospheric oxygen, increased nutrient supply from intense volcanic and mountain-building activity, and the expansion of plankton, which provided a richer food base for marine ecosystems. A more controversial hypothesis links the event to the break-up of a large asteroid in the asteroid belt around 466 million years ago, which delivered abundant meteorites to Earth and may have influenced climate through dust in the upper atmosphere [3].

sections.heading: Climatic/Environmental Changes
sections.body:
The Ordovician world was characterised by some of the highest sea levels in Earth's history. Broad, shallow epicontinental seas covered large parts of the continents of Laurentia, Baltica, Siberia, and Gondwana, providing vast areas of habitat for marine life. These seas varied widely in depth, temperature, and sediment type, creating a mosaic of environments.

Gradual global cooling through the Ordovician was a key environmental trend. As temperatures fell, the oceans became better oxygenated and steeper temperature gradients developed between the equator and the poles. These gradients encouraged the development of distinct faunal provinces, adding to the overall diversity of life.

The Ordovician was also a time of intense tectonic and volcanic activity. Island arcs and mountain belts formed along the margins of several continents, including the Taconic orogeny in eastern North America. Weathering of these new mountains and volcanic rocks supplied nutrients to the oceans, supporting greater productivity and the expansion of plankton communities.

sections.heading: Biological Impact
sections.body:
The GOBE saw spectacular diversification across many groups. Articulate brachiopods became the dominant filter feeders on the seafloor, while bryozoans, crinoids, and other echinoderms built complex communities. Tabulate and rugose corals appeared and, together with stromatoporoid sponges, began to construct the first large metazoan reefs.

In the water column, graptolites, acritarchs, and other plankton diversified, while nautiloid cephalopods, some reaching several metres in length, became top predators. Trilobites also diversified, although they became less dominant relative to other groups. The first jawless fishes with bony armour became more widespread, and early vertebrates diversified in marine environments.

Ecosystems became more complex in structure. Organisms occupied a wider range of living positions above and below the seafloor, a process known as tiering, and new modes of life such as burrowing and boring became more common. Food webs grew more intricate, with more trophic levels and greater ecological specialisation, and the overall biomass and productivity of marine ecosystems increased [1].

sections.heading: Legacy
sections.body:
The GOBE established the Paleozoic evolutionary fauna that dominated marine ecosystems for more than 200 million years, until its devastation in the Permian–Triassic extinction. Many of the groups that diversified during the Ordovician, including brachiopods, crinoids, and corals, remained central to marine life throughout the Silurian, Devonian, Carboniferous, and Permian.

The event also had consequences beyond the oceans. Around the same time, the first land plants — simple, non-vascular forms related to modern liverworts — began to colonise the land, as recorded by fossil spores of Middle Ordovician age [4]. This marked the beginning of the transformation of terrestrial environments that would later support forests and animal life.

The GOBE ended with the end-Ordovician mass extinction, which removed a large proportion of the newly evolved species. However, the ecological foundations laid during the event largely survived, and the diversification of the Ordovician remains one of the defining episodes in the history of marine life.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Cambrian explosion was a remarkable episode of evolutionary innovation during which most of the major groups of animals appeared in the fossil record. Beginning around 538.8 million years ago at the start of the Cambrian period and continuing for roughly 20 to 25 million years, it saw the rapid emergence of animals with complex bodies, hard skeletons, eyes, limbs, and sophisticated behaviours.

Before the Cambrian, animal life was largely restricted to simple forms such as sponges and the enigmatic soft-bodied organisms of the Ediacaran biota. During the Cambrian explosion, representatives of nearly all modern animal phyla, including arthropods, molluscs, brachiopods, echinoderms, and chordates, appear in the rock record, many in forms that look strikingly unfamiliar.

The event is documented by exceptional fossil sites known as Lagerstätten, which preserve soft tissues as well as hard parts. The most famous are the Burgess Shale of British Columbia, about 508 million years old, and the Chengjiang biota of Yunnan, China, about 518 million years old. These sites provide an extraordinary window into the earliest complex animal ecosystems [1].

sections.heading: Causes & Triggers
sections.body:
The causes of the Cambrian explosion have been debated since Charles Darwin, who regarded the sudden appearance of animal fossils as a challenge to his theory of gradual evolution [1]. Today, most researchers view the event as the result of a combination of environmental, genetic, and ecological factors rather than a single trigger.

Environmental changes likely played an important role. A rise in oxygen levels in the atmosphere and oceans during the late Neoproterozoic and early Cambrian may have allowed larger, more active animals to evolve. Changes in ocean chemistry, including increased concentrations of calcium and other ions possibly linked to weathering during the Great Unconformity, may have encouraged the evolution of mineralised skeletons [2].

Genetic and developmental innovations were also crucial. The evolution of complex gene regulatory networks, including Hox genes that control body patterning, provided the toolkit needed to build diverse body plans. Ecological interactions, particularly the emergence of predation, likely acted as a powerful driver, prompting an evolutionary 'arms race' that favoured armour, spines, burrowing, and improved senses such as vision. Molecular clock studies suggest that many animal lineages originated earlier in the Ediacaran, with the Cambrian explosion representing their ecological rise and fossilisation [3].

sections.heading: Climatic/Environmental Changes
sections.body:
The Cambrian explosion followed a period of profound environmental upheaval. The late Neoproterozoic had been marked by extreme 'Snowball Earth' glaciations, during which ice may have covered much of the planet. By the start of the Cambrian, the climate had become generally warm, with high sea levels and little or no polar ice.

Rising sea levels during the early Cambrian flooded the continental margins, creating extensive shallow marine habitats that provided ideal settings for the diversification of animals. The break-up of the supercontinent Rodinia and the assembly of Gondwana created new coastlines and ocean basins, increasing the variety of environments available.

Geochemical evidence, including fluctuations in carbon isotopes, records major disturbances to the carbon cycle during the early Cambrian. Oxygen levels in the oceans appear to have fluctuated, with episodes of oxygenation that may have coincided with pulses of diversification. The development of burrowing behaviour, known as the 'Cambrian substrate revolution', also transformed the seafloor, replacing the microbial mats of the Precambrian with mixed, oxygenated sediments.

sections.heading: Biological Impact
sections.body:
The Cambrian explosion produced an astonishing diversity of animals. Arthropods were especially prominent, with trilobites becoming one of the most abundant and diverse groups. Other arthropods included Anomalocaris, a large predator up to a metre long with grasping appendages and compound eyes, and a wide range of smaller forms such as Marrella and Waptia.

Many Cambrian animals were unusual and difficult to classify. Opabinia had five eyes and a long flexible proboscis, Hallucigenia was a spiny worm-like creature related to modern velvet worms, and Wiwaxia was covered in scales and spines. Such organisms are often interpreted as early relatives of living groups, revealing how modern body plans were assembled step by step.

The Cambrian explosion also saw the appearance of the earliest chordates, the group that includes vertebrates. Pikaia from the Burgess Shale and Myllokunmingia and Haikouichthys from Chengjiang represent some of the earliest known members of this lineage. Reef-building archaeocyathid sponges, early brachiopods, molluscs, and echinoderms further diversified the ecosystems of the time.

sections.heading: Legacy
sections.body:
The Cambrian explosion established the basic body plans of animal life that have persisted to the present day. Almost all of the major groups of animals living today can trace their origins to this interval, and subsequent evolution has largely involved variations on the themes established during the Cambrian.

The event also laid the foundations for complex ecosystems. Predator–prey relationships, food webs with multiple levels, and ecological interactions such as competition and symbiosis became established during the Cambrian, setting the stage for the further diversification of life during the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event.

The Cambrian explosion remains one of the most intensively studied events in the history of life. Discoveries at sites such as the Burgess Shale, Chengjiang, and more recently the Qingjiang biota of China continue to transform our understanding of early animal evolution [4]. The event raises fundamental questions about the processes that drive evolutionary innovation and the interplay between life and its environment.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Late Permian, also known as the Lopingian epoch, was the final epoch of the Permian period and of the Paleozoic era, lasting from about 259.5 to 251.9 million years ago [1]. It is divided into two stages, the Wuchiapingian and the Changhsingian, and its rocks are best known from southern China, where the boundary sections that define the end of the Paleozoic are preserved [1].

The Late Permian opened in the aftermath of the end-Guadalupian (Capitanian) extinction, which had struck tropical marine life and many terrestrial vertebrate groups. Over the following millions of years, life on land and in the sea rebuilt diverse communities, and the therapsids came to dominate terrestrial ecosystems across the supercontinent Pangaea.

The epoch ended with the Permian–Triassic extinction, often called the 'Great Dying', the most severe mass extinction in Earth's history. Triggered largely by the vast eruptions of the Siberian Traps, it eliminated around 90 percent of marine species and about 70 percent of terrestrial vertebrate species, closing the Paleozoic and setting the stage for the Mesozoic [2, 3].

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
The climate of the Late Permian was generally warm, and it became increasingly hot and arid as the epoch progressed. The great ice sheets of the Late Paleozoic Ice Age had long since disappeared, and there is little evidence for permanent polar ice. The enormous size of Pangaea produced a strongly continental climate, with extreme seasonal temperature swings and intense 'megamonsoon' circulation along its coasts [3].

The interior of the supercontinent was dominated by vast deserts and evaporite basins, while higher latitudes in both hemispheres supported cooler, wetter conditions in which forests and coal swamps persisted. Seasonal rivers and floodplains, such as those of the Karoo Basin of southern Africa, preserve a rich record of life in these semi-arid environments.

At the very end of the epoch, the eruption of the Siberian Traps released enormous quantities of carbon dioxide, methane, and sulfur gases. Global temperatures rose sharply, perhaps by 8–10 °C [4], and the oceans became warmer, more acidic, and widely depleted in oxygen, driving the catastrophic end-Permian extinction.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
During the Late Permian, nearly all of Earth's continental crust was assembled into the supercontinent Pangaea, which stretched from high southern latitudes to the northern polar regions. The vast global ocean Panthalassa surrounded it, while the Paleo-Tethys Ocean formed a wedge-shaped embayment on its eastern side.

A string of continental fragments known as the Cimmerian terranes, including parts of what are now Turkey, Iran, Tibet, and Southeast Asia, had rifted from the northern margin of Gondwana and was drifting northwards across the Tethys. Behind them, the Neo-Tethys Ocean was opening. The North and South China blocks lay as separate islands in the eastern Tethys, fringed by carbonate platforms and reefs.

In northern Pangaea, the Zechstein Sea, a shallow restricted basin covering parts of what are now northern Europe, repeatedly evaporated to leave thick deposits of salt and gypsum. Towards the end of the epoch, the Siberian Traps erupted across what is now northern Russia, covering millions of square kilometres with basaltic lava.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
The flora of the Late Permian reflected the drying trend that had begun earlier in the period. Seed plants dominated most landscapes, as their seeds and pollen allowed them to reproduce without the standing water required by spore-bearing plants. Conifers, cycads, ginkgophytes, and the extinct peltasperms were widespread in the drier regions of the supercontinent.

In the southern continents of Gondwana, the flora was dominated by Glossopteris, a woody seed plant with tongue-shaped leaves that formed extensive forests and contributed to thick coal deposits in Australia, India, Antarctica, and southern Africa. In the north, the Angaran flora of Siberia and the Cathaysian flora of China contained distinctive assemblages, with Cathaysia retaining lycopsid and tree-fern swamp forests.

The end-Permian extinction devastated land plants. The Glossopteris forests disappeared, coal formation ceased worldwide for millions of years in the so-called 'coal gap' [3], and in many regions the vegetation was replaced by communities of lycopsids such as Pleuromeia and by spore-producing plants adapted to disturbed environments.

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
The terrestrial fauna of the Late Permian was dominated by therapsids, the synapsid group that would later give rise to mammals. Herbivorous dicynodonts such as Dicynodon were extraordinarily abundant, while predatory gorgonopsians such as Inostrancevia, which reached about 3.5 metres in length, were the apex predators of the time [3].

Other important land animals included the large, armoured, plant-eating pareiasaurs such as Scutosaurus, and a variety of temnospondyl amphibians living in rivers and lakes. Early archosauromorphs, including Archosaurus from Russia, appeared near the end of the epoch, foreshadowing the rise of the reptiles that would later dominate the Mesozoic.

In the oceans, brachiopods, crinoids, bryozoans, rugose and tabulate corals, fusulinid foraminifera, and ammonoids flourished on reefs and shelves. The last trilobites survived until the end of the Permian. The end-Permian extinction wiped out these groups entirely or reduced them to a handful of survivors, transforming marine ecosystems permanently.

sections.heading: Synapsid Evolution
sections.body:
The Late Permian was a crucial time in the evolution of synapsids, the lineage that includes mammals and their extinct relatives. By this epoch the earlier pelycosaur-grade synapsids had largely disappeared, and the more advanced therapsids dominated terrestrial ecosystems worldwide.

The cynodonts, the therapsid group that would eventually give rise to mammals, first appeared in the Late Permian. Early forms such as Procynosuchus and Dvinia already showed features such as a secondary palate, which allowed breathing while chewing, enlarged temporal openings for stronger jaw muscles, and teeth differentiated into incisors, canines, and cheek teeth. Some researchers suggest that these animals may have had elevated metabolic rates and perhaps fur.

The end-Permian extinction hit synapsids hard, with gorgonopsians, most dicynodonts, and many other groups disappearing. However, a few lineages survived, including the dicynodont Lystrosaurus and several cynodonts and therocephalians. These survivors carried the synapsid lineage into the Triassic, where cynodonts would eventually give rise to the first true mammals.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Middle Permian, also known as the Guadalupian epoch, lasted from about 274.4 to 259.5 million years ago. It is divided into three stages, the Roadian, Wordian, and Capitanian, and takes its name from the Guadalupe Mountains of Texas and New Mexico, where spectacular fossil reefs of this age are exposed [1].

The Middle Permian was a time of major turnover in terrestrial ecosystems. The pelycosaur-grade synapsids that had dominated the Early Permian declined, and the therapsids rapidly diversified to become the dominant land vertebrates [2]. A short period of reduced diversity at this transition is sometimes called 'Olson's Gap', though its significance is debated.

The epoch ended with the end-Guadalupian or Capitanian extinction, around 260 million years ago. This event, possibly linked to the eruption of the Emeishan Traps in southern China, caused heavy losses among tropical marine organisms such as fusulinids, corals, and brachiopods, and also affected land animals, including the dinocephalians [3].

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
The climate of the Middle Permian was generally warm and became progressively drier. The last remnants of the Late Paleozoic Ice Age had largely disappeared by the start of the epoch, although some glacial deposits in eastern Australia suggest that small ice masses may have persisted at high southern latitudes [4].

The immense size of Pangaea created strongly seasonal, continental conditions. The tropical interior was dominated by deserts and red beds, while monsoonal climates prevailed along the margins of the Tethys Ocean. Higher latitudes in both hemispheres were cooler and wetter, supporting forests and the formation of coal.

Toward the end of the epoch, the Emeishan volcanic eruptions released large amounts of carbon dioxide and sulfur gases into the atmosphere. These eruptions have been linked to episodes of rapid warming, ocean acidification, and changes in the carbon cycle that coincided with the end-Guadalupian extinction [3]. A fall in sea level at around the same time also reduced shallow marine habitats.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
During the Middle Permian, Pangaea was fully assembled, stretching from the south polar region to high northern latitudes. The Central Pangean Mountains, raised during the earlier collision of Gondwana and Laurussia, ran across the equatorial region, while the Uralian mountains joined Europe to Siberia along the supercontinent's northern side.

The Paleo-Tethys Ocean formed a large embayment on the eastern side of Pangaea. During this epoch the Cimmerian terranes began to rift away from the northern margin of Gondwana, opening the Neo-Tethys Ocean behind them. North China, South China, and Indochina lay as separate landmasses within the Tethys, surrounded by warm, shallow seas.

In western North America, the Delaware Basin was rimmed by the Capitan Reef, a massive reef complex built by sponges, algae, and bryozoans that is now exposed in the Guadalupe Mountains. Elsewhere, extensive evaporite and red-bed deposits accumulated in basins across the arid interior of the supercontinent.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
The flora of the Middle Permian was dominated by seed plants, which were well suited to the drier conditions that had spread across Pangaea. Conifers, cycads, ginkgophytes, and seed ferns such as the peltasperms and gigantopterids were widespread, and in many regions they replaced the spore-bearing plants of the Carboniferous coal swamps.

The floras of the world were divided into distinct provinces. In Gondwana, Glossopteris and related plants formed extensive forests in cool, wet lowlands and contributed to thick coal deposits. The Angaran province of Siberia had its own distinctive cordaitalean-dominated forests, while the Cathaysian province of China retained tropical swamp forests with lycopsids, tree ferns, and the large-leaved gigantopterids.

In the equatorial belt of Euramerica, the vegetation was adapted to seasonal drought. Plants with thick cuticles, reduced leaves, and other water-conserving features became common, and the older coal swamp flora survived only in isolated, wetter refuges.

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
The terrestrial fauna of the Middle Permian was marked by the rise of the therapsids. Among the most distinctive were the dinocephalians, a group of large herbivores and carnivores such as Moschops, Estemmenosuchus, and Anteosaurus, some of which reached the size of a modern rhinoceros. Many had thickened skulls that may have been used in head-butting contests.

The earliest dicynodonts and gorgonopsians also appeared in this epoch, alongside therocephalians and early pareiasaurs. Rich fossil assemblages from the Karoo Basin of South Africa and the Ural region of Russia record these communities in detail. Temnospondyl amphibians, some of which were large aquatic predators, remained important in rivers and lakes.

In the seas, reefs built by sponges, bryozoans, and calcareous algae flourished, along with diverse brachiopods, crinoids, ammonoids, and large fusulinid foraminifera. The end-Guadalupian extinction severely affected many of these groups, especially the large fusulinids and tropical reef communities, and on land it brought the dinocephalians to extinction [3].

sections.heading: Synapsid Evolution
sections.body:
The Middle Permian saw one of the most important transitions in the history of synapsids: the replacement of the earlier pelycosaur-grade forms by the therapsids. Although the origins of the therapsids probably lie in the Early Permian, the oldest well-dated therapsid fossils come from the early part of the Middle Permian, and the group diversified rapidly thereafter [2].

Therapsids differed from their predecessors in several ways. Their limbs were held more beneath the body, allowing a more efficient gait, and their skulls had larger temporal openings for stronger jaw muscles. Many had well-developed canine teeth, and some evidence suggests that their metabolic rates were higher than those of the earlier synapsids [2].

By the end of the epoch, the major therapsid lineages, including the dinocephalians, anomodonts, gorgonopsians, therocephalians, and the ancestors of the cynodonts, had all become established. Although the end-Guadalupian extinction removed the dinocephalians, the remaining lineages went on to dominate terrestrial ecosystems during the Late Permian.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Early Permian, also known as the Cisuralian epoch, was the first epoch of the Permian period, lasting from about 298.9 to 274.4 million years ago. It is divided into four stages, the Asselian, Sakmarian, Artinskian, and Kungurian, and takes its name from the western slopes of the Ural Mountains, where marine rocks of this age are well exposed [1].

The Early Permian was a time of transition. It began during the final phase of the Late Paleozoic Ice Age, when large ice sheets still covered much of southern Gondwana, and ended in a much warmer and drier world [2]. These climatic changes had profound effects on plant and animal life across the supercontinent Pangaea.

On land, the Early Permian was the age of the pelycosaur-grade synapsids, such as the sail-backed Dimetrodon and Edaphosaurus, which were the dominant large land animals of the time [3]. Amphibians and early reptiles were also diverse, and the famous red beds of Texas preserve one of the richest records of Early Permian terrestrial life.

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
At the beginning of the Early Permian, Earth was still in the grip of the Late Paleozoic Ice Age. Extensive ice sheets covered parts of southern Africa, South America, Antarctica, India, and Australia, and global sea levels fluctuated as the ice advanced and retreated [2]. Atmospheric carbon dioxide levels were low, possibly comparable to those of the present day.

During the Sakmarian and Artinskian stages, the ice sheets began to shrink, and by the end of the epoch most of the glaciers had disappeared. This deglaciation was accompanied by rising carbon dioxide levels and global warming, and the climate of Pangaea became increasingly arid [2].

In the tropics, the wet, swampy conditions of the Carboniferous gave way to seasonal climates with long dry seasons. Red beds, evaporites, and desert sandstones became widespread across the equatorial regions of the supercontinent, while the higher latitudes became cool and temperate as the ice retreated.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
During the Early Permian, the continents had nearly completed their assembly into the supercontinent Pangaea. Gondwana in the south had collided with Laurussia in the north, raising the Central Pangean Mountains, a chain that included the Appalachians and the Variscan mountains of Europe and North Africa.

In the north-east, the collision of Siberia and Kazakhstania with Europe was completing the formation of the Ural Mountains, joining these landmasses to the rest of the supercontinent. To the east, the Paleo-Tethys Ocean formed a large embayment, while North China, South China, and other Asian blocks remained separate landmasses within it.

The vast global ocean Panthalassa covered most of the rest of the planet. Shallow seas still flooded parts of the continental interiors, especially in western North America, where marine and coastal deposits interfinger with the terrestrial red beds of Texas, Oklahoma, and New Mexico.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
The flora of the Early Permian reflected the shift from the humid conditions of the Carboniferous to a drier, more seasonal climate. In the tropical regions of Euramerica, the great coal swamp forests of giant lycopsids had largely disappeared, replaced by vegetation dominated by tree ferns, seed ferns, cordaitaleans, and early conifers such as Walchia.

In Gondwana, the retreat of the ice sheets allowed the spread of the Glossopteris flora, which colonised the cool, wet lowlands left behind by the glaciers. These plants formed extensive forests that would later produce thick coal deposits across the southern continents.

In China, the Cathaysian province retained a humid tropical flora with lycopsids, tree ferns, and the distinctive gigantopterids, some of the earliest plants with complex, net-veined leaves. Fossil forests buried by volcanic ash in Inner Mongolia, sometimes called a 'Pompeii' of plants, preserve an entire Early Permian peat-forest ecosystem [4].

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
The terrestrial fauna of the Early Permian was dominated by pelycosaur-grade synapsids. The predator Dimetrodon, which reached more than 3 metres in length and bore a tall sail on its back, was the apex predator of many ecosystems, while the herbivorous Edaphosaurus had a similar sail. Large herbivorous caseids such as Cotylorhynchus were also present.

Amphibians were still diverse and important. The temnospondyl Eryops was a large, heavily built predator of rivers and swamps, while the lepospondyl Diplocaulus had a distinctive boomerang-shaped head. Early reptiles, including the captorhinids and the bipedal bolosaurid Eudibamus, were also present, as were the reptile-like seymouriamorphs and diadectids.

In the oceans, fusulinid foraminifera, brachiopods, bryozoans, crinoids, and ammonoids were abundant. The small aquatic reptile Mesosaurus lived in a shallow inland sea between what are now South America and Africa, and its fossils were later used as evidence for continental drift.

sections.heading: Synapsid Evolution
sections.body:
The Early Permian was the heyday of the pelycosaur-grade synapsids, an informal group of early synapsids that includes the ancestors of the therapsids and, ultimately, of mammals. These animals were distinguished from other early amniotes by a single opening behind the eye on each side of the skull, which anchored powerful jaw muscles.

Several distinct lineages flourished during the epoch. The sphenacodontids, including Dimetrodon, were the dominant predators and are thought to be the closest relatives of the therapsids. The edaphosaurids and caseids were among the first large terrestrial herbivores, while the varanopids were agile, lizard-like predators. The sails of Dimetrodon and Edaphosaurus may have helped regulate body temperature or served for display.

Toward the end of the epoch, the pelycosaur-grade synapsids began to decline, and the first therapsids probably appeared [3]. The transition between these groups is poorly documented, but it marked the beginning of the line that would lead through the cynodonts to the first mammals.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Late Carboniferous, corresponding to the Late Pennsylvanian epoch, lasted from about 307 to 298.9 million years ago. It comprises two stages, the Kasimovian and the Gzhelian, both named after localities in Russia, and it was the final part of the Carboniferous period before the beginning of the Permian [1].

The Late Carboniferous was a time of major environmental change. It began shortly after the Carboniferous Rainforest Collapse, a series of events in which the vast tropical coal swamp forests of Euramerica fragmented and were largely replaced by drier, more seasonal vegetation [2]. This change had important consequences for the animals that lived in these forests.

At the same time, the Late Paleozoic Ice Age continued, with large ice sheets covering parts of the southern supercontinent Gondwana. Repeated advances and retreats of these ice sheets caused sea levels to rise and fall many times, producing the rhythmic layers of coal, shale, and limestone known as cyclothems [3].

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
The climate of the Late Carboniferous was shaped by the Late Paleozoic Ice Age, the longest glaciation of the last 500 million years [3]. Ice sheets extended across large parts of southern Gondwana, and atmospheric carbon dioxide levels were low. Oxygen levels were exceptionally high, possibly above 30 percent, compared with about 21 percent today [4].

The glaciers waxed and waned in response to cyclical changes in Earth's orbit, and sea levels rose and fell by tens of metres as a result. During glacial phases, the tropics tended to be drier, while interglacial phases brought wetter conditions and the spread of coastal swamps [3].

Over the course of the epoch, the equatorial regions of Pangaea became increasingly seasonal and arid. The ever-wet climate that had supported the great coal forests gave way to a climate with pronounced dry seasons, and red beds became more common in the tropical interior. This drying trend continued into the Permian.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
During the Late Carboniferous, the supercontinent Pangaea was nearing completion. Gondwana in the south had collided with Laurussia in the north, raising the Central Pangean Mountains, a long chain that ran across the equator and included the Appalachians, the Mauritanides of West Africa, and the Variscan mountains of Europe.

In the north-east, Siberia and Kazakhstania were converging with eastern Europe, beginning to raise the Ural Mountains. To the east lay the Paleo-Tethys Ocean, while the vast Panthalassic Ocean covered most of the rest of the globe. North China and South China remained separate continents within the Tethys region.

Shallow seas periodically flooded the low-lying interiors of North America and Europe as sea levels rose during interglacial phases, and retreated during glacial phases. In western North America, the uplift of the Ancestral Rocky Mountains created new highlands and basins, while foreland basins along the Variscan and Appalachian ranges collected thick sequences of coal-bearing sediments.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
The flora of the Late Carboniferous was strongly affected by the Carboniferous Rainforest Collapse. The giant lycopsids, such as Lepidodendron and Sigillaria, which had dominated the coal swamps of earlier times, declined sharply in the tropical regions of Euramerica, although they persisted in some areas, particularly in China.

Tree ferns such as Psaronius became the dominant plants of many remaining wetlands, and they formed much of the coal of this time. Seed ferns, horsetails such as Calamites, and cordaitaleans were also common, while early conifers, better adapted to dry conditions, became increasingly widespread in upland and seasonally dry environments.

In the cooler southern regions of Gondwana, vegetation was sparse near the ice sheets, while in Siberia the Angaran flora was dominated by cordaitaleans adapted to temperate conditions. The shift towards seed plants during this epoch foreshadowed the vegetation of the Permian.

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
The Late Carboniferous was a time of giant arthropods. The high oxygen levels of the atmosphere are thought to have allowed insects and other arthropods to grow to enormous sizes [4]. The griffinfly Meganeura, a relative of modern dragonflies, had a wingspan of about 70 centimetres, and the millipede-like Arthropleura could reach more than 2 metres in length.

Amphibians were the most diverse land vertebrates. Temnospondyls and lepospondyls lived in swamps and rivers, while early amniotes, including both reptiles and synapsids, were becoming more common. The breakup of the rainforests into isolated patches is thought to have favoured amniotes, which were better adapted to drier conditions [2].

In the seas, brachiopods, crinoids, bryozoans, rugose and tabulate corals, and fusulinid foraminifera were abundant on shallow shelves. Ammonoids, nautiloids, and a wide variety of fish, including many unusual cartilaginous fish such as the eugeneodonts and the iniopterygians, swam in the oceans.

sections.heading: Rise of Amniotes
sections.body:
The Late Carboniferous was an important time in the early evolution of the amniotes, the group of vertebrates that includes reptiles, birds, and mammals. Amniotes lay eggs with protective membranes and shells, allowing them to reproduce away from water, and they have waterproof skin that reduces water loss.

By this epoch, the two main branches of amniotes had already split: the sauropsids, which would give rise to reptiles and birds, and the synapsids, which would give rise to mammals. Early synapsids such as the ophiacodontids, edaphosaurids, and sphenacodontids grew larger and more diverse, while early diapsid reptiles such as Petrolacosaurus appeared.

The Carboniferous Rainforest Collapse is thought to have accelerated the rise of amniotes. As the wet forests fragmented, amphibians, which depend on water for reproduction, suffered, while amniotes, better able to cope with dry conditions, spread and diversified [2]. Herbivory among land vertebrates also became established, with forms such as Edaphosaurus and the diadectids feeding on plants.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Middle Carboniferous, corresponding to the Early and Middle Pennsylvanian epochs, lasted from about 323.4 to 307 million years ago. It comprises the Bashkirian and Moscovian stages and follows the boundary between the Mississippian and Pennsylvanian subperiods, which is marked by a major fall in sea level linked to the growth of ice sheets in Gondwana [1].

This interval represents the peak of the great coal swamp forests. Vast wetlands covered the tropical lowlands of Euramerica, and the plant material buried in them formed the coal deposits of North America and Europe that later fuelled the Industrial Revolution. The name Carboniferous, meaning 'coal-bearing', reflects the importance of these deposits.

The Middle Carboniferous was also a time of important evolutionary events on land, including the appearance of the first amniotes, the radiation of winged insects, and the rise of giant arthropods. Towards its end, the Carboniferous Rainforest Collapse began to fragment the tropical forests.

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
The climate of the Middle Carboniferous was dominated by the Late Paleozoic Ice Age. Large ice sheets covered much of southern Gondwana, including parts of South America, southern Africa, Antarctica, India, and Australia. Atmospheric carbon dioxide levels were low, partly because of the enormous amounts of carbon being buried in the coal swamps [2].

Atmospheric oxygen levels rose to some of the highest values in Earth's history, possibly exceeding 30 percent. This was due to the burial of plant material faster than it could decompose, as well as photosynthesis by the extensive forests. The high oxygen levels may have made wildfires more frequent and allowed arthropods to grow to large sizes.

The equatorial regions were warm and very humid, with high rainfall throughout the year that sustained the coal forests. Repeated glacial and interglacial cycles caused large changes in sea level, producing cyclothems, the alternating layers of marine and non-marine sediments characteristic of this time.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
During the Middle Carboniferous, the supercontinent Pangaea was in the process of forming. Gondwana was colliding with Laurussia along a broad zone that stretched from what is now the south-eastern United States through north-western Africa to central Europe. This collision, known as the Variscan or Alleghanian orogeny, raised a vast mountain chain across the equator [3].

The Rheic Ocean, which had once separated Gondwana and Laurussia, was closing, while the Paleo-Tethys Ocean lay to the east. Siberia and Kazakhstania were still separate continents to the north-east, gradually approaching Europe [3]. The Panthalassic Ocean covered most of the rest of the globe.

Along the margins of the new mountain chain, low-lying foreland basins and coastal plains provided ideal settings for the coal swamps. Rivers carried sediment from the rising mountains into deltas and lagoons, and shallow seas repeatedly flooded and retreated across these lowlands as sea levels changed.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
The Middle Carboniferous was the time of the great coal swamp forests [2]. These forests were dominated by giant lycopsids, such as Lepidodendron and Sigillaria, which could reach heights of 30 metres or more. These trees had trunks covered with diamond-shaped leaf scars and were anchored by spreading root systems known as Stigmaria.

Other important plants included giant horsetails such as Calamites, which grew along river banks and in disturbed areas, as well as tree ferns, seed ferns, and the cordaitaleans, tall seed plants with long, strap-like leaves that grew in coastal and drier settings. Early conifers also appeared in upland environments.

The coal swamps were remarkably productive, and the slow decay of plant material in their waterlogged soils led to the formation of thick deposits of peat, which later became coal. In regions such as North America, Europe, and China, these coal deposits are among the most important in the world.

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
The Middle Carboniferous saw a major diversification of terrestrial animals. Winged insects, which first appeared in the earlier Carboniferous, radiated rapidly and included early relatives of dragonflies, mayflies, cockroaches, and the extinct palaeodictyopterans with their piercing mouthparts. Giant arthropods such as Arthropleura and early griffinflies roamed the forests.

Amphibians were the dominant land vertebrates. Large temnospondyls lived in swamps and rivers, while lepospondyls included small, snake-like, and lizard-like forms. Fossil sites such as Mazon Creek in Illinois and Joggins in Nova Scotia preserve remarkable snapshots of life in and around the coal swamps.

In the seas, brachiopods, crinoids, bryozoans, and corals flourished, and fusulinid foraminifera became abundant. Ammonoids diversified, and the oceans contained a wide variety of fish, including early ray-finned fish and many unusual sharks and their relatives, such as the stethacanthids with their distinctive dorsal fins.

sections.heading: Rise of Amniotes
sections.body:
The Middle Carboniferous saw the appearance of the first amniotes, one of the most important events in vertebrate evolution. Amniotes produce eggs with a set of protective membranes, including the amnion, that allow the embryo to develop on land. This freed them from the need to return to water to breed, as amphibians must.

The oldest known amniote is Hylonomus, a small, lizard-like animal about 20 centimetres long, found inside the fossilised stumps of lycopsid trees at Joggins in Nova Scotia, dated to about 318 million years ago [4]. Other early amniotes, such as Paleothyris, were similar small insectivores.

Remarkably, the split between the two major amniote lineages, the sauropsids and the synapsids, had already occurred by the end of this interval. Early synapsids such as Archaeothyris and Echinerpeton are known from rocks around 310 to 306 million years old. These small animals were the distant ancestors of the mammals, while the sauropsids would give rise to reptiles and birds.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Early Carboniferous, corresponding to the Mississippian subperiod, lasted from about 358.9 to 323.4 million years ago. It is divided into three stages, the Tournaisian, Visean, and Serpukhovian, and takes its name from the Mississippi River valley in North America, where limestones of this age are widely exposed [1].

The Early Carboniferous began in the aftermath of the Late Devonian extinctions, including the Hangenberg event at the end of the Devonian, which devastated marine ecosystems and early vertebrates [2]. The recovery from these extinctions shaped the ecosystems of the Carboniferous, both in the seas and on land.

The Early Carboniferous was a time of extensive shallow tropical seas, in which vast limestone deposits formed from the remains of crinoids and other marine organisms. On land, tetrapods diversified and spread into new environments, and the first great forests of lycopsids began to develop in coastal wetlands.

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
The climate of the Early Carboniferous was initially warm, but it cooled over the course of the subperiod. The spread of forests across the continents increased the weathering of rocks and the burial of organic carbon, which drew carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere and contributed to global cooling.

Glacial deposits in South America show that ice sheets had formed in southern Gondwana by the beginning of the Carboniferous [2], and glaciation became more extensive during the later Visean and Serpukhovian stages. This marked the onset of the main phase of the Late Paleozoic Ice Age, which would last until the Permian [3].

The tropical regions remained warm and generally humid, supporting extensive carbonate platforms in the shallow seas and the growth of swamp forests along coasts. Atmospheric oxygen levels were rising, setting the stage for the exceptionally high oxygen levels of the later Carboniferous.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
During the Early Carboniferous, the continents were beginning to come together to form Pangaea. The southern supercontinent Gondwana lay mainly in the Southern Hemisphere, with the South Pole located in southern Africa or Antarctica. To the north lay Laurussia, also known as Euramerica, which straddled the equator.

The Rheic Ocean between Gondwana and Laurussia was narrowing as the two landmasses converged, and the first stages of the Variscan orogeny were raising mountains in what is now Europe. Siberia, Kazakhstania, North China, and South China were separate continents, scattered around the Paleo-Tethys and Panthalassic oceans.

Sea levels were high during much of the Early Carboniferous, and shallow, warm seas covered large areas of North America, Europe, and Asia. In these seas, thick limestone deposits accumulated, forming the Carboniferous Limestone of Britain and the Mississippian limestones of North America, while coastal lowlands supported the first extensive coal-forming swamps.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
The flora of the Early Carboniferous was dominated by spore-bearing plants, although seed plants were also present. Lycopsids, such as early forms of Lepidodendron, formed forests in wetland environments, and they would later become the dominant trees of the great coal swamps. Horsetails, ferns, and fern-like plants were also common.

The first seed plants had appeared in the Late Devonian, and during the Early Carboniferous they diversified into a wide range of seed ferns. These plants were able to colonise drier habitats than spore-bearing plants, as their seeds did not need water for fertilisation.

The vegetation of the Early Carboniferous recovered from the effects of the end-Devonian extinction, which had affected land plants as well as animals. Fossil plant sites in Scotland, such as Pettycur, preserve detailed records of these early Carboniferous floras, often buried by volcanic ash.

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
The seas of the Early Carboniferous were dominated by crinoids, or sea lilies, which formed vast 'meadows' on the sea floor. So abundant were they that this time is sometimes called the 'Age of Crinoids'. Brachiopods, bryozoans, rugose and tabulate corals, and blastoids were also common, and ammonoids diversified after the end-Devonian extinction.

The fish fauna changed dramatically after the Late Devonian extinctions. The armoured placoderms had disappeared, and cartilaginous fish, such as sharks and their relatives, became very diverse [2]. The Bear Gulch Limestone of Montana preserves an extraordinary array of these animals, including the bizarre Falcatus and Stethacanthus. Ray-finned fish also diversified.

On land, arthropods such as scorpions and millipedes were present, and the first winged insects appeared towards the end of the subperiod. Early tetrapods lived in and around swamps, rivers, and lakes, and some were becoming increasingly adapted to life on land.

sections.heading: Early Tetrapods
sections.body:
The Early Carboniferous was a crucial time in the evolution of tetrapods, the four-limbed vertebrates. The first part of the subperiod was long thought to be almost devoid of tetrapod fossils, a gap known as 'Romer's Gap'. However, recent discoveries in Scotland and elsewhere have revealed a diverse range of early tetrapods from this time [4].

These early tetrapods included both aquatic and more terrestrial forms. Some, such as Pederpes from Scotland, had feet that appear adapted for walking on land. By the Visean stage, a wide variety of tetrapods had appeared, including early temnospondyls, baphetids, and the reptile-like anthracosaurs. The East Kirkton site in Scotland preserves animals such as Westlothiana and Balanerpeton, along with scorpions and millipedes.

During the Early Carboniferous, the lineages that would give rise to modern amphibians and amniotes probably diverged. Some tetrapods, such as Casineria, show features that may indicate a close relationship to the amniotes, foreshadowing the appearance of the first true amniotes in the following epoch.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Late Devonian was the final epoch of the Devonian period, lasting from about 382.7 to 358.9 million years ago. It is divided into two stages, the Frasnian and the Famennian, and it closed the long interval often called the 'Age of Fishes'. The epoch saw the culmination of several great evolutionary trends that had begun earlier in the Devonian, including the spread of the first true forests and the emergence of four-limbed vertebrates.

The Late Devonian is best known for the Late Devonian extinction, one of the 'Big Five' mass extinctions in Earth's history. Rather than a single catastrophe, it consisted of a series of pulses, the most severe of which, the Kellwasser event, occurred near the Frasnian–Famennian boundary around 372 million years ago. A later crisis, the Hangenberg event, struck at the very end of the Devonian [1].

Together these events eliminated an estimated 70 to 80 percent of marine species. Tropical reef ecosystems were devastated, and many groups of armoured fishes vanished entirely, reshaping the course of vertebrate evolution as the world entered the Carboniferous period.

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
The climate of the Late Devonian was generally warm, but it became increasingly unstable as the epoch progressed. During the Frasnian, global temperatures were high, with tropical sea surface temperatures that may have exceeded 30 °C, and shallow seas supported vast reef systems [2]. Atmospheric carbon dioxide levels were still several times higher than today, although they were declining.

One leading hypothesis links this decline to the spread of land plants. As deep-rooted trees colonized the continents, they accelerated chemical weathering of rocks, drawing carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere, and released nutrients that washed into the oceans. These nutrient pulses may have triggered algal blooms and widespread ocean anoxia, recorded in black shales around the world [3].

By the Famennian, the climate had cooled significantly. Glaciers began to form in the southern part of Gondwana, particularly in what is now South America, and by the end of the Devonian a short but significant glaciation was under way. This cooling, combined with sea level fluctuations and anoxia, is widely thought to have contributed to the Hangenberg extinction [1].

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
During the Late Devonian, the continents were gradually converging toward the formation of the supercontinent Pangaea. The great southern continent Gondwana, made up of present-day South America, Africa, Antarctica, Australia, and India, lay across the southern hemisphere and was slowly moving northward.

Near the equator lay Laurussia, also known as Euramerica or the 'Old Red Sandstone Continent', which had formed earlier through the collision of Laurentia, Baltica, and Avalonia. Its eroding mountain belts shed enormous quantities of red sediment into river systems and basins, forming the famous Old Red Sandstone deposits of Britain, Greenland, and eastern North America. Siberia, Kazakhstania, and the North and South China blocks formed separate landmasses to the north and east.

Between Gondwana and Laurussia, the Rheic Ocean was narrowing as the two continents approached one another, a process that would eventually build the Variscan and Appalachian mountain belts. Sea levels were high for much of the epoch, flooding continental interiors with warm, shallow epicontinental seas, although they fluctuated sharply toward the end of the Devonian.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
The Late Devonian witnessed one of the most important transformations in the history of life on land: the rise of the first forests. The progymnosperm Archaeopteris, a tree that combined woody trunks like those of conifers with fern-like reproduction by spores, became widespread across the world [3]. It could reach heights of 20 to 30 metres and possessed extensive root systems and flat, leaf-bearing branches.

Archaeopteris forests transformed landscapes. Their roots stabilized river banks and soils, changing the way rivers flowed, while their fallen leaves and branches contributed large amounts of organic matter to soils and waterways [3]. Alongside them grew early lycopsids, sphenopsids related to modern horsetails, and a variety of fern-like plants.

The Late Devonian also saw a major reproductive innovation: the first seed plants appeared during the Famennian. Early seed-bearing plants such as Elkinsia and Moresnetia were small and shrubby, but the seed freed plants from the need for water to reproduce, eventually allowing vegetation to spread into drier upland habitats in the following periods.

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
The seas of the Late Devonian were dominated by fishes of remarkable diversity. The placoderms, armoured jawed fishes, reached their peak, and the arthrodire Dunkleosteus, which may have exceeded 4 metres in length, was among the largest predators of its time. Its jaws bore self-sharpening bony plates capable of delivering a powerful bite. Sharks such as Cladoselache, along with ray-finned and lobe-finned fishes, also thrived.

Invertebrate life was equally rich. Vast reefs built by stromatoporoid sponges and tabulate and rugose corals covered shallow tropical seafloors, while ammonoids, brachiopods, crinoids, trilobites, and conodonts were abundant. These reef ecosystems were among the most extensive in Earth's history before the Kellwasser event caused their collapse.

On land, arthropods such as millipedes, early arachnids, and wingless hexapods lived among the growing forests. The Late Devonian extinction struck hardest in the tropics and among shallow-water organisms: reef builders, many trilobite groups, and nearly all jawless fishes disappeared, and the placoderms were entirely extinct by the end of the epoch [1].

sections.heading: Rise of Tetrapods
sections.body:
The Late Devonian was the time when vertebrates first developed limbs with digits, one of the most significant transitions in the history of life. The ancestors of tetrapods were lobe-finned fishes known as tetrapodomorphs, which possessed robust, bony fins and lived in shallow, oxygen-poor waters such as river channels, lagoons, and swamps.

The fossil record documents this transition in remarkable detail. Eusthenopteron was a fully aquatic fish with limb-like bones in its fins, while Panderichthys and the famous Tiktaalik, discovered in Arctic Canada and dated to around 375 million years ago, had flattened heads, mobile necks, and sturdy fins capable of supporting their bodies in shallow water [4]. Tiktaalik is often described as a 'fishapod' because it combines features of both fishes and tetrapods.

By the Famennian, true early tetrapods had appeared. Acanthostega and Ichthyostega, known from East Greenland, possessed limbs with up to seven or eight digits, yet they retained gills and tail fins and probably spent most of their time in water. Fossil trackways from Poland, however, suggest that limbed vertebrates may have existed even earlier, in the Middle Devonian. The descendants of these early tetrapods would go on to give rise to amphibians, reptiles, and mammals.
