sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Middle Devonian was the second epoch of the Devonian period, lasting from about 393.3 to 382.7 million years ago. It is divided into two stages, the Eifelian and the Givetian, named after rock sequences in Germany and France. Although shorter than the epochs before and after it, the Middle Devonian was a time of exceptional biological richness both in the oceans and on land.

The epoch is often regarded as the heart of the 'Age of Fishes', when jawed fishes of many kinds diversified and spread through marine and freshwater environments around the world. At the same time, the land was being transformed by the appearance of the first tree-sized plants and the earliest forests.

The Middle Devonian also saw the greatest development of reefs in the entire Paleozoic era [1]. Warm, shallow seas covered much of the continents, supporting enormous reef complexes. The epoch was punctuated by several smaller extinction events, including the Kačák event near the Eifelian–Givetian boundary and the Taghanic event late in the Givetian, both associated with episodes of ocean anoxia and sea level change [2].

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
The climate of the Middle Devonian was warm and largely free of polar ice. Estimates suggest that tropical sea surface temperatures were around 25 to 30 °C, comparable to or slightly warmer than those of today. Atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations were considerably higher than at present, although they were beginning a long decline that would continue through the rest of the Paleozoic.

The warm climate allowed reef-building organisms to flourish far from the equator, and evaporite deposits and red beds indicate that arid conditions prevailed in some subtropical regions. Elsewhere, especially along the margins of Laurussia, humid conditions supported extensive river systems and coastal swamps.

The spread of larger plants with deeper roots during the Middle Devonian had begun to change the chemistry of the atmosphere and oceans. Enhanced weathering of rocks removed carbon dioxide from the air and delivered nutrients to the sea. Some researchers link these changes to the episodes of oxygen depletion recorded in marine black shales, such as those of the Kačák and Taghanic events, which caused regional extinctions among ammonoids, brachiopods, and corals [2].

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
In the Middle Devonian, the Earth's landmasses were arranged in a pattern that foreshadowed the later assembly of Pangaea. The supercontinent Gondwana dominated the southern hemisphere, with the South Pole lying over what is now southern Africa or South America. Its northern margin bordered the narrowing Rheic Ocean.

Straddling the equator lay Laurussia, formed by the earlier collision of Laurentia, Baltica, and Avalonia during the Caledonian orogeny. The Caledonian mountains, stretching from Scandinavia through Scotland to Greenland and the Appalachians, were being eroded, filling intermontane basins with the thick river and lake deposits of the Old Red Sandstone. Siberia, Kazakhstania, and the Chinese blocks were scattered to the north and east, separated by smaller seaways.

Sea levels were high and rising through much of the Middle Devonian, and broad epicontinental seas flooded large parts of North America, Europe, northern Africa, and Australia. These shallow, sunlit seas formed ideal settings for reef growth, and their deposits are preserved today in places such as the Canning Basin of Western Australia, the Eifel region of Germany, and western Canada [1].

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
The Middle Devonian marked a turning point in the evolution of land plants, as vegetation grew from low-lying ground cover into the first forests. Among the earliest tree-like plants were the cladoxylopsids, such as Wattieza and Calamophyton. These plants had tall, unbranched trunks topped by crowns of branchlets, resembling modern tree ferns or palms, and reached heights of around 8 to 10 metres [3].

Fossil stumps of Wattieza discovered at Gilboa in New York State, dating to around 385 million years ago, represent some of the oldest known forest trees [3]. Excavations at Gilboa and at Cairo, New York, have revealed entire forest floors with rooting systems, showing that complex woodland ecosystems with several kinds of trees already existed by the end of the epoch [4].

Other important plants included early lycopsids, the ancestors of the giant scale trees of the Carboniferous, as well as early sphenopsids and the first progymnosperms, such as Archaeopteris, which appeared near the end of the Givetian [4]. Smaller plants including zosterophylls and trimerophytes still grew along wet lowlands, and soils became deeper and richer as root systems expanded.

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
The marine life of the Middle Devonian was among the most diverse of the Paleozoic era. Enormous reefs were built by stromatoporoid sponges together with tabulate and rugose corals, forming structures that in some regions stretched for hundreds of kilometres [1]. These reefs supported a wealth of brachiopods, crinoids, bryozoans, gastropods, and bivalves.

Trilobites were still common, and the Middle Devonian produced some of the most elaborate forms ever known, including heavily spined species such as Walliserops and Dicranurus, preserved in spectacular detail in the rocks of Morocco. Ammonoids, which had first appeared in the Early Devonian, diversified rapidly and became important both as predators and as index fossils for dating rocks. Eurypterids, or sea scorpions, persisted in brackish and freshwater habitats.

On land, arthropods were the dominant animals. Millipedes, centipedes, and early arachnids such as trigonotarbids inhabited the growing forests and leaf litter. Fossils from Gilboa include some of the earliest known pseudoscorpions and spider-like arachnids, providing evidence that complex terrestrial food webs were becoming established.

sections.heading: Age of Fishes
sections.body:
The Middle Devonian is the epoch most closely associated with the 'Age of Fishes', when fishes reached a peak of diversity and variety unmatched at any earlier time. Nearly every major group of early fishes was present, living side by side in seas, lagoons, rivers, and lakes.

The placoderms, armoured fishes with jointed head and trunk shields, were the most abundant and diverse vertebrates. They ranged from bottom-dwelling antiarchs such as Bothriolepis and Pterichthyodes, with their box-like armour and jointed pectoral appendages, to predatory arthrodires that grew steadily larger. Jawless fishes, including heterostracans and osteostracans, persisted but were in decline.

The bony fishes were also diversifying rapidly. Ray-finned fishes such as Cheirolepis appeared in freshwater habitats, while lobe-finned fishes, including lungfishes, coelacanths, and the tetrapodomorphs such as Osteolepis, became widespread. The exceptionally preserved fish beds of the Orcadian Basin in Scotland record entire lake communities of these animals. Early sharks and spiny acanthodians were also common. This flourishing of fish lineages laid the foundations for nearly all later vertebrate life, including the tetrapods.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Early Devonian was the first epoch of the Devonian period, lasting from about 419.2 to 393.3 million years ago. It is divided into three stages: the Lochkovian, the Pragian, and the Emsian, the first two named after localities in the Czech Republic. At more than 25 million years long, it was the longest of the three Devonian epochs.

The Early Devonian followed the Silurian period without any major extinction, and many Silurian groups continued to flourish. However, it was a time of important evolutionary change. Jawed fishes began to replace the jawless fishes that had dominated earlier seas, ammonoids made their first appearance, and life on land expanded from narrow coastal fringes into a wider range of habitats.

The epoch is especially famous for the Rhynie Chert of Scotland, a deposit of silica-rich hot spring sediments dating to around 407 million years ago [1]. It preserves early plants, fungi, and animals in microscopic, cellular detail, providing an extraordinary snapshot of one of the earliest terrestrial ecosystems [1].

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
The climate of the Early Devonian was generally warm, with high atmospheric carbon dioxide levels, perhaps ten times greater than those of today or more. There is little evidence for large polar ice sheets, and tropical sea surface temperatures were probably warm, with some geochemical studies suggesting values above 30 °C during parts of the epoch.

Large regions of the continents were arid or semi-arid. Laurussia, lying in the southern tropics and subtropics, experienced strongly seasonal conditions, and its interior basins accumulated the red sandstones, conglomerates, and caliche-bearing soils characteristic of the Old Red Sandstone. These deposits record rivers that flowed intermittently, alternating between floods and dry seasons.

Throughout the Early Devonian, land plants were still small and shallow-rooted, so their influence on global climate was limited compared with later times. Nevertheless, the gradual spread of vegetation and the development of the first true soils began the long process by which plants would draw down atmospheric carbon dioxide, contributing to the cooling trend of the later Devonian.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
At the start of the Devonian, the collision of Laurentia, Baltica, and the microcontinent Avalonia had recently been completed during the Caledonian orogeny, creating the continent of Laurussia. Its suture zone was marked by a lofty mountain chain stretching from Norway across Scotland and Greenland to the northern Appalachians, and these mountains were actively eroding throughout the Early Devonian.

The vast southern continent Gondwana covered much of the southern hemisphere, with the South Pole located over its western part. The Rheic Ocean separated Gondwana from Laurussia, while a number of smaller terranes, including parts of what are now central Europe, lay within or along its margins. Siberia and the North and South China blocks were isolated landmasses situated nearer the equator.

Sea levels were relatively low at the beginning of the Devonian following the Silurian, but they rose through the Early Devonian, flooding continental margins with shallow seas. In areas such as the Hunsrück region of Germany, fine muds deposited in these seas preserved remarkable fossils, including starfish, crinoids, and arthropods with their soft tissues replaced by pyrite.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
The plants of the Early Devonian were mostly small, rarely more than a metre tall, and grew in moist lowland environments near rivers, lakes, and coasts. Many were simple vascular plants without true leaves or roots. Rhyniophytes such as Rhynia and Aglaophyton had branching, leafless green stems that carried out photosynthesis and bore spore capsules at their tips.

Other groups were more advanced. The zosterophylls, which bore kidney-shaped sporangia along their stems, are considered the ancestors of lycopsids, the club mosses. Small lycopsids such as Asteroxylon, which had tiny leaf-like scales, appeared during the epoch, while trimerophytes such as Psilophyton developed more complex branching patterns and are thought to be ancestors of ferns, horsetails, and seed plants.

Alongside these plants grew the enigmatic Prototaxites, a towering organism up to 8 metres tall that is now generally interpreted as a giant fungus [2]. The Rhynie Chert also shows that many early plants formed partnerships with mycorrhizal fungi, which helped them absorb water and nutrients, a relationship that remains essential to most plants today [1].

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
The seas of the Early Devonian supported rich communities of invertebrates. Brachiopods were especially abundant and diverse, and corals, stromatoporoids, bryozoans, and crinoids built reefs and carpeted shallow seafloors. Trilobites remained common, while graptolites, which had been abundant in earlier periods, dwindled and became largely extinct in the open ocean during this epoch.

One of the most important events of the Early Devonian was the first appearance of ammonoids, coiled cephalopods that evolved from straight-shelled bactritid ancestors during the Emsian [3]. Ammonoids would go on to become one of the most successful groups of marine animals, surviving until the end of the Cretaceous. The Early Devonian also saw a broader shift known as the 'Devonian nekton revolution', in which swimming animals became increasingly common in the water column [3].

In freshwater and brackish environments, eurypterids reached enormous sizes. Jaekelopterus, known from Early Devonian rocks of Germany, may have reached around 2.5 metres in length, making it one of the largest arthropods ever to have lived [4]. Jawless fishes, placoderms, and acanthodians shared these waters.

sections.heading: Terrestrial Colonization
sections.body:
The Early Devonian was a crucial chapter in the colonization of land by life. Although plants, fungi, and some arthropods had already established themselves along the margins of the continents in the Silurian, the Early Devonian saw these pioneers form more complex and interconnected ecosystems.

The Rhynie Chert provides the most complete picture of this early terrestrial world. It preserves not only plants but also fungi, lichens, algae, and a variety of tiny animals. These include mites, springtail-like hexapods such as Rhyniella, trigonotarbid arachnids, and the oldest known harvestman [1]. Some plant stems show wounds and fungal infections, while others preserve evidence of animals feeding on spores and plant tissues. The fossil insect Rhyniognatha, also from Rhynie, may represent one of the earliest known insects.

As plants spread inland, they began to modify their environment. Their stems and rhizomes helped bind sediments, slowing erosion and allowing the development of more stable soils. Decomposing plant material supported populations of detritivores such as millipedes, which in turn were preyed upon by centipedes and arachnids. These developments laid the groundwork for the forested ecosystems of the Middle and Late Devonian and for the eventual move of vertebrates onto land.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Late Silurian encompasses the final two epochs of the Silurian period, the Ludlow and the Pridoli, spanning from about 427.4 to 419.2 million years ago. The Ludlow is named after the town of Ludlow in Shropshire, England, while the Pridoli takes its name from a locality near Prague in the Czech Republic. The Pridoli is unusual in being the only epoch in the geological timescale that is not subdivided into stages.

The Late Silurian was a time of warm seas and growing biological diversity. Marine ecosystems had largely recovered from the Late Ordovician mass extinction, and reefs, brachiopods, and early fishes flourished. At the same time, life on land was taking hold, with the earliest well-documented vascular plants appearing in coastal habitats.

The epoch was not without its crises. The Lau event, during the middle Ludlow around 424 million years ago, was a significant extinction episode that affected conodonts, graptolites, trilobites, and early fishes [1]. It coincided with one of the largest positive carbon isotope excursions of the Phanerozoic, reflecting major disturbances to the global carbon cycle [1].

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
The climate of the Late Silurian was mostly warm, as the Earth continued to emerge from the glaciations of the Late Ordovician and Early Silurian. Remnant glaciers may have persisted at high latitudes in Gondwana, particularly in what is now South America, but large ice sheets had largely disappeared. Tropical sea surface temperatures likely ranged from around 25 to 30 °C or more.

The climate was nevertheless subject to significant fluctuations. The Lau event in the Ludlow coincided with a drop in sea level and evidence for cooler conditions, and possibly with changes in ocean circulation and oxygen levels. Some researchers suggest that a brief glacial episode in Gondwana may have contributed to these disturbances [1].

On land, conditions in many regions were arid, especially in the tropical and subtropical belts. Thick deposits of evaporites, including salt and gypsum, accumulated in restricted basins such as the Michigan Basin of North America, where seawater evaporated under a hot, dry climate. These deposits reflect a world in which warm, shallow seas alternated with hypersaline lagoons and dry coastal plains.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
In the Late Silurian, the continents of Laurentia and Baltica, together with the microcontinent Avalonia, were completing their collision to form Laurussia. This collision, known as the Caledonian orogeny, raised a great mountain chain along the line of the former Iapetus Ocean, which was now almost entirely closed. Remains of this mountain belt can be traced today through Scandinavia, Scotland, Ireland, Greenland, and Newfoundland.

Laurussia lay across the equator and in the southern tropics, while the immense continent Gondwana occupied the southern hemisphere and extended over the South Pole. Between them lay the Rheic Ocean, which had widened during the Ordovician and Silurian. Siberia, North China, South China, and several smaller terranes lay scattered across the tropics and the northern hemisphere, which was otherwise covered by the vast Panthalassic Ocean.

Sea levels were generally high during the Silurian but fell toward the end of the period. Broad shallow seas still covered parts of North America, Europe, and Asia, and their sediments preserve abundant fossils. Famous sites include the Ludlow bone beds of England and the fossil-rich Eurypterid beds of New York State.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
The Late Silurian is a key interval in the history of land plants. Although spores from simple plants are known from the Ordovician, the first unambiguous fossils of vascular plants appear in the Silurian. The best known is Cooksonia, a small plant only a few centimetres tall with slender, leafless, forking stems topped by tiny spore-bearing capsules [2].

Cooksonia and similar plants lacked true roots and leaves and probably grew in damp habitats such as river margins and coastal mudflats. They possessed water-conducting tissues and a waxy cuticle with stomata, adaptations that allowed them to survive out of water [2]. Remarkably, the larger lycopsid Baragwanathia, with spirally arranged leaves, is known from rocks in Australia that may date to the Ludlow, suggesting that plant evolution on land was already more advanced than once thought.

Alongside vascular plants, the land was colonized by non-vascular plants related to liverworts and mosses, by algae, and by fungi and lichen-like organisms. Prototaxites, a large tree-like fungus, also first appeared in the Late Silurian. Together, these organisms formed low mats and patches of vegetation, mostly confined to wet lowlands.

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
The seas of the Late Silurian teemed with invertebrate life. Reefs built by tabulate and rugose corals, stromatoporoid sponges, and bryozoans were widespread in tropical waters, providing habitats for brachiopods, crinoids, gastropods, and nautiloids. Trilobites remained common, though they were less dominant than in earlier periods. Graptolites, colonial planktonic animals, continued to evolve rapidly and are widely used to date Silurian rocks.

The Late Silurian was the heyday of the eurypterids, or sea scorpions. These predatory arthropods were abundant in shallow marine, brackish, and lagoonal environments, and some, such as the pterygotids, grew to well over a metre in length. Exceptionally preserved eurypterids from New York State and Estonia show their paddle-like swimming legs and grasping claws.

On land, the first arthropods were appearing. Fossils from the Ludlow of England and from Scotland include early myriapods such as Pneumodesmus, one of the oldest known air-breathing land animals [3], as well as trigonotarbid arachnids. These animals probably fed on decaying plant material and on each other, forming some of the earliest terrestrial food chains.

sections.heading: Jawed Fish Evolution
sections.body:
The Late Silurian was a critical time in the evolution of jawed vertebrates, or gnathostomes. Although jawless fishes such as the armoured heterostracans, osteostracans, and anaspids were still widespread and diverse, jawed fishes were becoming increasingly common and varied. The evolution of jaws, derived from the skeletal arches that supported the gills, allowed vertebrates to feed in new ways and opened up a wide range of ecological opportunities.

Several major groups of jawed fishes were already present. Acanthodians, small fishes with sharp spines in front of their fins, were common in both marine and freshwater environments. Placoderms, the armoured fishes, are well represented in Late Silurian rocks of China, where fossils such as Entelognathus show a surprising combination of placoderm armour and bony-fish-like jaw bones, shedding light on the origins of modern jaws.

The bony fishes, or osteichthyans, had also appeared by this time. Guiyu oneiros, from the Ludlow of Yunnan, China, is one of the oldest known bony fishes and among the earliest jawed vertebrates preserved nearly complete [4]. It combines features of both ray-finned and lobe-finned fishes, showing that the two great lineages of bony fishes had already begun to diverge [4]. Their descendants would dominate the waters of the Devonian and ultimately give rise to the tetrapods.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Middle Silurian corresponds to the Wenlock epoch, which lasted from about 433.4 to 427.4 million years ago. It is divided into two stages, the Sheinwoodian and the Homerian, and is named after Wenlock Edge, a limestone escarpment in Shropshire, England, where rocks of this age are exposed and richly fossiliferous.

The Wenlock was a time of warm, shallow seas and flourishing reef ecosystems. Marine life had substantially recovered from the Late Ordovician mass extinction, and communities of corals, brachiopods, crinoids, and trilobites were diverse and widespread. The famous Wenlock Limestone of England, with its abundant fossil reefs, is one of the classic records of Silurian marine life.

The epoch was also punctuated by biological crises. The Ireviken event, at the start of the Wenlock, and the Mulde event, in the Homerian, both caused significant extinctions among conodonts, graptolites, and trilobites [1]. These events were associated with marked changes in ocean chemistry and carbon isotope ratios, reflecting the sensitivity of Silurian ecosystems to environmental change [2].

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
The climate of the Middle Silurian was generally warm, with high atmospheric carbon dioxide levels and widespread tropical conditions. The great glaciations of the Late Ordovician and Early Silurian had largely ended, although some ice may have persisted in the polar regions of Gondwana. Tropical sea surface temperatures were probably similar to or somewhat warmer than those of today.

Nevertheless, the Wenlock climate was not entirely stable. Geochemical evidence, including oxygen and carbon isotope records from limestones in Gotland, Sweden, and elsewhere, indicates that the Ireviken and Mulde events coincided with periods of cooling, falling sea level, and changes in ocean circulation [1]. Some researchers propose that brief glacial episodes in Gondwana may have driven these fluctuations.

The oceans of the Silurian may have alternated between distinct states, with episodes of warm, stratified, poorly oxygenated waters giving way to cooler, well-mixed conditions. These shifts are thought to have influenced the productivity of marine ecosystems and the extinction and diversification of planktonic organisms such as graptolites and acritarchs.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
During the Middle Silurian, the continents of Laurentia and Baltica were converging as the Iapetus Ocean that had separated them continued to close. The microcontinent Avalonia had already docked with Baltica, and its collision with Laurentia was well under way, beginning to raise the mountains of the Caledonian orogeny in what is now Scotland, Scandinavia, and Greenland.

Laurentia, forming much of present-day North America, straddled the equator, while Baltica lay in the southern tropics. Gondwana, by far the largest landmass, lay mostly in the southern hemisphere, with the South Pole situated beneath what is now central Africa or South America. Siberia, the North and South China blocks, and other smaller terranes lay in tropical and subtropical latitudes, surrounded by the Panthalassic and Paleo-Tethys oceans.

Sea levels during the Wenlock were high, and shallow epicontinental seas covered large areas of Laurentia and Baltica. Vast carbonate platforms developed in these seas, including the reef-rich limestones of Gotland in Sweden, the Niagara Escarpment of North America, and the Wenlock Edge of England.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
Life on land during the Middle Silurian was still in its early stages. The continents were largely barren of complex vegetation, but microbial mats, algae, and lichen-like organisms covered damp surfaces, helping to weather rocks and form primitive soils. Fossil spores show that non-vascular plants, related to modern liverworts and mosses, were well established in moist environments.

The Wenlock contains some of the earliest known fossils of vascular plants. Cooksonia, a tiny plant with forking, leafless stems tipped with spore capsules, first appears in rocks of this age in Ireland [3]. Its water-conducting tissues and protective cuticle represent important adaptations that would allow later plants to grow taller and spread into drier habitats.

In the oceans, the base of the food chain was formed by photosynthetic plankton, including acritarchs, which were abundant and diverse, as well as various seaweeds and calcareous algae. Algae also contributed to building reefs and carbonate sediments in shallow tropical seas. Changes in acritarch diversity are recorded across the extinction events of the Wenlock, reflecting the disruption of marine productivity.

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
The marine fauna of the Middle Silurian was rich and diverse. Reefs constructed by tabulate corals such as Favosites and Halysites, along with rugose corals, stromatoporoid sponges, and bryozoans, flourished in shallow tropical seas. These reefs housed abundant brachiopods, crinoids, gastropods, bivalves, and cephalopods, including straight-shelled nautiloids.

Trilobites were common, and the Wenlock Limestone of England yields well-known species such as Calymene blumenbachii, often called the 'Dudley Bug' after the town where it was frequently collected. Graptolites remained important members of the plankton, though many species were lost during the Ireviken and Mulde events. Conodonts, eel-like animals known mainly from their tiny tooth-like elements, also suffered repeated extinctions.

The Herefordshire Lagerstätte of England, dating to around 430 million years ago, preserves small marine invertebrates in remarkable three-dimensional detail. Its fossils include early arthropods, molluscs, worms, sponges, and echinoderms, revealing aspects of Silurian life that are rarely preserved [4]. On land, evidence for animals is sparse, but small arthropods may have begun exploring coastal environments.

sections.heading: Marine Evolution
sections.body:
The Middle Silurian was a period of steady evolutionary innovation in the oceans, shaped by a cycle of extinction and recovery. The Ireviken event, at the beginning of the Wenlock, eliminated around 80 percent of conodont species and about half of all trilobite species in some regions, along with many graptolites [1]. Later, the Mulde event struck graptolites particularly hard, reducing them to only a handful of species before they recovered and diversified again [2].

Despite these setbacks, marine ecosystems became increasingly complex. Reef systems expanded and became more structurally diverse, providing new ecological niches for a wide variety of organisms. Eurypterids, or sea scorpions, diversified in nearshore and brackish waters and became important predators, while cephalopods occupied the role of active hunters in open waters.

Vertebrates also continued to evolve during the Wenlock. Jawless fishes such as the armoured heterostracans and osteostracans, and the more lightly built anaspids and thelodonts, were widespread in coastal seas. At the same time, early jawed fishes, including acanthodians and the first placoderms, were becoming more common. Isolated scales and teeth from Wenlock rocks suggest that the major lineages of jawed vertebrates were diversifying, setting the stage for the explosion of fish diversity in the Devonian.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Early Silurian corresponds to the Llandovery epoch, the first epoch of the Silurian period, lasting from about 443.8 to 433.4 million years ago. It is divided into three stages, the Rhuddanian, the Aeronian, and the Telychian, and is named after the town of Llandovery in Wales, where rocks of this age were first studied in the nineteenth century.

The Llandovery began in the aftermath of the Late Ordovician mass extinction, the second most severe extinction in Earth's history, which eliminated around 85 percent of marine species [1]. The extinction was closely linked to a major glaciation centred on Gondwana, and the beginning of the Silurian was marked by the melting of these ice sheets and a substantial rise in sea level [1].

The Early Silurian was therefore a time of recovery and rebuilding. Surviving groups of marine organisms diversified to fill vacant ecological niches, and graptolites, brachiopods, corals, and other groups rapidly radiated. By the end of the epoch, marine ecosystems had largely regained their former richness, and reefs once again flourished in tropical seas.

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
At the beginning of the Early Silurian, the Earth was emerging from the Late Ordovician glaciation, known as the Hirnantian glaciation. Ice sheets that had covered much of North Africa and parts of South America were retreating, though glaciers persisted in Gondwana into the Llandovery, particularly in what is now Brazil and Bolivia.

As the ice melted, the climate warmed and global sea levels rose by tens of metres, flooding the margins of the continents. Atmospheric carbon dioxide levels were high, and tropical seas were warm, allowing reef-building organisms to recover and spread. However, the warming was not uniform, and the Llandovery appears to have experienced several smaller glacial episodes, reflected in fluctuations in sea level and in carbon and oxygen isotope records.

The melting ice and rising seas also influenced ocean chemistry. During the early Llandovery, oxygen-poor waters spread across many continental shelves, leading to the deposition of organic-rich black shales in North Africa, the Middle East, and elsewhere. These shales are today among the most important source rocks for petroleum in the world, having generated a large share of the oil and gas of North Africa and Arabia [2].

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
In the Early Silurian, the supercontinent Gondwana dominated the southern hemisphere, extending from the tropics to the South Pole, which lay beneath what is now northern or central Africa. Its northern margin bordered the Rheic Ocean, which had opened during the Ordovician as the microcontinent Avalonia rifted away from Gondwana and drifted northward.

Laurentia, the core of present-day North America, lay across the equator, while Baltica, comprising much of northern Europe, lay to its east in the southern tropics. Between them, the Iapetus Ocean was narrowing as these continents and Avalonia converged. Their collision during the later Silurian would build the Caledonian mountains. Siberia, North China, and South China were separate landmasses situated in tropical latitudes, and the rest of the northern hemisphere was occupied by the vast Panthalassic Ocean.

The post-glacial rise in sea level flooded broad areas of the continents, creating extensive shallow seas. In Laurentia, Baltica, and South China, these seas supported carbonate platforms and early reef systems, while deeper waters accumulated graptolite-rich shales that are used today to subdivide Silurian time.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
During the Early Silurian, the land surface remained sparsely vegetated by modern standards. However, fossil spores show that plants had been present on land since the Middle Ordovician, and by the Llandovery they were widespread in moist environments [3]. These early land plants were small, non-vascular forms comparable to liverworts and mosses, growing as low mats and crusts in damp soils and near water.

The spores of this epoch include both cryptospores, typically found in tetrads or pairs and associated with the earliest land plants, and trilete spores, which are more typical of vascular plants. The increasing abundance of trilete spores through the Llandovery suggests that vascular plants were beginning to emerge, although their body fossils remain rare until later in the Silurian [3].

Alongside plants, fungi, lichens, and microbial communities colonized rock surfaces and contributed to the formation of early soils. In the oceans, photosynthetic plankton such as acritarchs and various algae formed the base of marine food webs. Their recovery after the Late Ordovician extinction was essential to the rebuilding of marine ecosystems during the Early Silurian.

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
The fauna of the Early Silurian was shaped by recovery from the Late Ordovician mass extinction. Groups that survived the extinction, including brachiopods, trilobites, corals, crinoids, and bryozoans, diversified as warm seas spread across the continental shelves. Brachiopods such as the pentamerids formed dense shell beds on shallow seafloors, and communities of these animals are often used to reconstruct Silurian water depths.

Graptolites, colonial planktonic organisms, underwent a dramatic radiation during the Llandovery. The monograptids, characterized by a single row of cups along a straight or coiled stipe, became dominant, and their rapid evolution makes them excellent index fossils. Spectacularly spiral forms such as Rastrites and Spirograptus appeared during this time.

Reefs, which had been severely affected by the extinction, began to re-establish themselves later in the epoch, built by tabulate and rugose corals and stromatoporoid sponges. Nautiloids, eurypterids, and early fishes also inhabited Llandovery seas. The Waukesha biota of Wisconsin, dating to the Telychian, preserves soft-bodied animals including worms, arthropods, and early relatives of horseshoe crabs.

sections.heading: Marine Evolution
sections.body:
The Early Silurian was a time of rapid evolutionary recovery in the oceans. The Late Ordovician mass extinction had removed many established groups and disrupted marine ecosystems, creating opportunities for survivors to diversify. Over several million years, marine biodiversity climbed back toward pre-extinction levels, with new species of brachiopods, corals, trilobites, and graptolites appearing in quick succession.

One of the most significant developments was the early diversification of vertebrates. Jawless fishes such as thelodonts, anaspids, heterostracans, and galeaspids, the last known especially from South China, were widespread in shallow seas and coastal waters. Scales and fragmentary remains also indicate that jawed fishes, including acanthodians and early chondrichthyans related to sharks, were present, although they remained small and relatively uncommon.

Recent discoveries from Chongqing, China, dating to around 436 million years ago, have dramatically improved knowledge of early jawed vertebrates. Fossils such as the placoderm-like Xiushanosteus and the shark relative Shenacanthus show that the major lineages of jawed fishes had already diverged by the Llandovery [4]. These findings suggest that the origin of jaws, one of the key innovations in vertebrate history, occurred earlier than previously thought, laying the foundation for the later dominance of jawed fishes in the Devonian seas.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Late Ordovician was the final epoch of the Ordovician period, lasting from about 458.4 to 443.8 million years ago. It is divided into three stages: the Sandbian, the Katian and the Hirnantian. The epoch saw marine life reach the peak of the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event, with the number of marine genera roughly tripling compared with the Cambrian [1].

Shallow tropical seas teemed with brachiopods, bryozoans, trilobites, crinoids, corals and cephalopods, and the first extensive reef systems built by tabulate corals, rugose corals and stromatoporoid sponges spread across the continental shelves. Jawless fishes were well established, and the first undisputed land plants, known from their spores, were slowly colonising damp ground along shorelines.

The epoch ended in catastrophe. The Late Ordovician mass extinction, the first of the 'Big Five' mass extinctions of the Phanerozoic, struck in two pulses during the Hirnantian stage and eliminated around 85 percent of marine species [2]. It was closely linked to a short but intense glaciation centred on the supercontinent Gondwana [2].

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
For most of the Late Ordovician, the global climate was warm, with high atmospheric carbon dioxide levels and sea levels among the highest of the entire Phanerozoic. Vast epicontinental seas flooded the interiors of Laurentia, Baltica and parts of Gondwana, producing widespread warm, shallow marine environments.

Through the Katian, however, the climate gradually cooled. Possible causes include enhanced weathering of newly uplifted volcanic mountain belts, such as those of the Taconic orogeny, which drew down carbon dioxide, and the spread of early land plants, which may have accelerated chemical weathering of silicate rocks. Sea surface temperatures in the tropics, estimated from oxygen isotopes in conodont teeth, fell by several degrees, perhaps from above 30 °C to the mid 20s °C.

In the Hirnantian, about 445 million years ago, this cooling culminated in a major glaciation. Ice sheets spread across North Africa and neighbouring parts of Gondwana, which lay over the South Pole, leaving glacial tillites and striated pavements in what is now the Sahara. Sea level fell by perhaps 50 to 100 metres, draining the shallow seas, before the ice rapidly melted again at the end of the epoch [3].

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
During the Late Ordovician, the largest landmass was the supercontinent Gondwana, which comprised present-day South America, Africa, Antarctica, Australia, India and Arabia. Gondwana stretched from the tropics to the South Pole, with northern Africa positioned over the pole itself.

Several smaller continents lay closer to the equator. Laurentia, the core of North America, straddled the equator, while Baltica and Siberia lay in the tropics and subtropics. Avalonia, a microcontinent that had rifted away from Gondwana, was drifting northward across the Rheic Ocean towards Baltica, steadily narrowing the Iapetus Ocean that separated these landmasses from Laurentia.

The margins of the Iapetus were sites of intense tectonic activity. Island arcs collided with the eastern edge of Laurentia during the Taconic orogeny, raising mountains in what is now the Appalachian region, and powerful explosive eruptions spread ash layers, now preserved as bentonites, across vast areas. The northern hemisphere was dominated by the immense Panthalassic Ocean, and continental interiors were almost entirely flooded by shallow seas.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
No unequivocal vascular plant fossils are known from the Late Ordovician [4], and photosynthesis in the oceans was carried out by a diverse array of algae and cyanobacteria. Microscopic organic-walled cysts called acritarchs, many of which were probably the resting stages of planktonic algae, were abundant and diverse, forming the base of marine food webs. Calcareous green and red algae, including dasycladaleans and solenoporaceans, grew in shallow tropical seas and contributed to reef and carbonate platform construction.

On land, the most important development was the continued spread of the earliest embryophytes, the ancestors of all modern land plants. These are known almost entirely from cryptospores, tiny spores arranged in pairs and fours with tough walls of sporopollenin, which allowed them to resist drying out [4]. Their parent plants were probably small, liverwort-like organisms that lived in damp habitats near water.

Microbial mats and crusts of cyanobacteria, fungi and possibly lichen-like associations likely covered moist surfaces of the land. Together with the early plants, these communities began to alter weathering and soil formation, and some researchers suggest that their effect on the carbon cycle may have contributed to the cooling that led to the Hirnantian glaciation.

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
Late Ordovician seas supported one of the richest marine faunas of the Palaeozoic. Articulate brachiopods were the most common shelled animals on the seafloor, alongside bryozoans, crinoids and other echinoderms, bivalves and gastropods. Trilobites remained diverse, with forms ranging from large-eyed swimmers to burrowing and spiny species.

Nautiloid cephalopods were the top invertebrate predators, and some endocerids possessed straight shells several metres long. Graptolites, colonial hemichordates that drifted in the plankton, were so abundant and evolved so rapidly that they are used to divide the period into fine biozones. Conodonts, small eel-like vertebrates known mainly from their tooth-like elements, were widespread.

Vertebrates were represented by jawless fishes, including armoured forms such as the arandaspids and astraspids, and early relatives of jawed fishes may already have appeared, as suggested by fragmentary scales. On land, there is evidence from trace fossils that small arthropods, possibly early millipede-like animals, were beginning to venture out of the water. The Hirnantian extinction devastated this fauna, particularly affecting graptolites, trilobites, brachiopods, conodonts and reef-building organisms.

sections.heading: Marine Evolution
sections.body:
The Late Ordovician represents the culmination of the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event, during which the 'Palaeozoic evolutionary fauna' replaced the trilobite-dominated communities of the Cambrian [1]. Filter-feeding animals such as brachiopods, bryozoans and crinoids built complex, tiered communities on the seafloor, while reefs developed a new architecture based on corals and stromatoporoids.

The Hirnantian mass extinction struck in two main phases. The first pulse occurred at the onset of glaciation, when falling sea levels drained shallow shelf habitats and cooling waters killed warm-adapted tropical species. The second pulse came as the ice sheets melted, when rising seas and the spread of oxygen-poor waters across the continental shelves eliminated many of the cold-adapted species that had survived the first phase [2].

In the aftermath, a distinctive cool-water brachiopod assemblage known as the Hirnantia fauna spread around the world. Despite the enormous loss of species, the extinction did not fundamentally reorganise marine ecosystems in the way later extinctions did, and the surviving groups, especially the brachiopods, corals and crinoids, rebounded during the Silurian to form communities broadly similar to those of the Ordovician.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Middle Ordovician was the second epoch of the Ordovician period, lasting from about 470 to 458.4 million years ago. It is divided into two stages, the Dapingian and the Darriwilian. This epoch was the time of the most rapid diversification during the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event, one of the most important radiations of animal life in Earth's history [1].

During the Middle Ordovician, the number of marine families and genera increased dramatically. Brachiopods, bryozoans, crinoids, bivalves, cephalopods and graptolites all diversified rapidly, and marine ecosystems became far more complex than those of the Cambrian, with more ecological niches and more tiered communities on the seafloor.

The epoch is also notable for a remarkable event in the solar system. Around 466 million years ago, the break-up of a large asteroid in the asteroid belt showered the Earth with meteorites for millions of years, and fossil meteorites are found in Middle Ordovician limestones in Sweden and elsewhere [2]. Some scientists have suggested that dust from this event may have influenced climate and evolution.

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
The early part of the Ordovician had been extremely hot, but by the Middle Ordovician the climate had cooled to more moderate levels. Oxygen isotope measurements from conodont fossils suggest that tropical sea surface temperatures fell from over 35 °C in the Early Ordovician to around 28 to 30 °C by the Darriwilian, similar to modern equatorial oceans [3].

This cooling may have been a key factor in the explosion of marine diversity, since many organisms could not tolerate the very high temperatures of earlier times. The causes of the cooling are debated, but they may include the drawdown of carbon dioxide through weathering of volcanic rocks, changes in ocean circulation, or the effects of extraterrestrial dust from the break-up of the L-chondrite parent body, which may have reduced the amount of sunlight reaching the surface [2].

Sea levels were generally high and rising during the Middle Ordovician, flooding large parts of the continents. The atmosphere contained much more carbon dioxide than today, and oxygen levels in the oceans and atmosphere appear to have been rising, which may also have favoured the evolution of larger and more active animals.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
In the Middle Ordovician, the supercontinent Gondwana dominated the southern hemisphere, extending from the equator across the South Pole. Australia, Antarctica and parts of China lay in the warm tropics along its northern margin, while North Africa and South America occupied high southern latitudes.

The smaller continents of Laurentia, Baltica and Siberia were separated from Gondwana and from each other by several oceans. Laurentia lay across the equator, while Baltica was moving northward from temperate southern latitudes into warmer waters. The Iapetus Ocean, between Laurentia and Baltica, was at or near its widest extent but had begun to close, with subduction zones and volcanic island arcs developing along its margins.

The microcontinent Avalonia, which included parts of present-day England, Wales, Newfoundland and New England, began to rift away from Gondwana during this time, opening the Rheic Ocean behind it. Widespread volcanism and the growth of island arcs, together with high sea levels, created a patchwork of shallow seas, carbonate platforms and deeper basins, providing a wide variety of habitats for marine life.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
Life in the Middle Ordovician remained almost entirely aquatic, and the primary producers were algae and cyanobacteria. The phytoplankton underwent its own diversification during this epoch, and acritarchs, the microscopic organic-walled cysts of single-celled algae, reached some of their highest levels of diversity in the Palaeozoic. This increase in plankton is thought to have supported the radiation of filter-feeding animals.

In shallow seas, calcareous algae, including early red and green algae, grew on carbonate platforms, and cyanobacteria continued to form microbial mats and stromatolites, though these were becoming less common as grazing animals increased in number. Algae such as receptaculitids, an enigmatic group probably related to green algae, formed large dish-shaped structures on the seafloor.

The Middle Ordovician also provides the oldest widely accepted evidence of land plants. Cryptospores from rocks in Argentina, dating to around 470 million years ago, indicate that small, simple plants related to liverworts had already begun colonising damp environments on land [4]. These earliest embryophytes lacked vascular tissues and true roots, but their spores had resistant walls that protected them from drying out.

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
Middle Ordovician seas contained a rapidly diversifying fauna. Brachiopods of many kinds became the dominant shelled animals of the seafloor, while bryozoans, which first appeared in the Early Ordovician, built branching and encrusting colonies. Crinoids and other echinoderms, including cystoids and early starfish, formed dense 'meadows' in some areas.

Trilobites were still abundant, though they now formed a smaller part of the overall fauna than in the Cambrian. Cephalopods diversified into many forms, and large straight-shelled endocerids, some reaching several metres in length, were among the largest animals of their time. Graptolites floated in great numbers in the open ocean and evolved rapidly, making them excellent index fossils.

Bivalves and gastropods became more diverse, and the first extensive reefs built by animals since the Early Cambrian, including early bryozoan, sponge and coral reefs, began to appear. Vertebrates were represented by conodonts and by early jawless fishes such as Sacabambaspis, a small armoured fish from South America with eyes positioned at the very front of its head. Ostracods, small bivalved crustaceans, also diversified rapidly.

sections.heading: Marine Evolution
sections.body:
The Middle Ordovician was the heart of the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event. During this time, the number of marine genera increased several-fold, and the 'Palaeozoic evolutionary fauna', dominated by brachiopods, bryozoans, crinoids, corals and cephalopods, rose to dominance in place of the trilobite-rich 'Cambrian evolutionary fauna' [1].

This radiation was not driven by the origin of new body plans, since most animal phyla had appeared in the Cambrian, but by an increase in diversity within existing groups and the occupation of new ecological niches. Animals began to live higher above the seafloor, burrow deeper into sediments and swim in the open water column, and food webs became more complex as plankton diversified.

Scientists have proposed many causes for this event, including the cooling of the climate, rising oxygen levels, high sea levels that created extensive shallow seas, increased nutrients from volcanic activity and mountain building, and the dispersal of continents, which isolated populations and promoted the formation of new species. The meteorite shower from the break-up of an asteroid may also have played a role, though this remains debated [1, 2].

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Early Ordovician was the first epoch of the Ordovician period, lasting from about 485.4 to 470 million years ago. It is divided into two stages, the Tremadocian and the Floian. The beginning of the Ordovician is defined by the first appearance of the conodont Iapetognathus fluctivagus in rocks at Green Point in Newfoundland, Canada [1].

The Early Ordovician followed a series of extinction events at the end of the Cambrian, and marine life was in a phase of recovery and renewal. During this epoch the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event began, as many groups of animals that would dominate Palaeozoic seas started to diversify.

The Early Ordovician is famous for its exceptionally preserved fossils from the Fezouata Formation in Morocco, which reveal that many soft-bodied animals typical of the Cambrian, including giant filter-feeding radiodonts and early relatives of arthropods, survived well into the Ordovician alongside newer groups such as graptolites, bryozoans and diverse cephalopods [2].

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
The climate of the Early Ordovician was very hot. Oxygen isotope data from conodont fossils suggest that tropical sea surface temperatures may have exceeded 35 °C and possibly reached 40 °C at times, conditions that would have been stressful for many marine animals [3]. Atmospheric carbon dioxide levels were many times higher than today, and there is no evidence of polar ice.

Sea levels were rising throughout the epoch, flooding the low-lying interiors of the continents and creating broad, warm, shallow seas. In these seas, thick sequences of carbonate rocks, including limestones and dolomites, accumulated on extensive platforms, particularly in Laurentia, which lay across the equator.

During the later part of the Early Ordovician, the climate began to cool gradually, a trend that continued into the Middle Ordovician [3]. This cooling is considered one of the possible triggers for the great diversification of marine life, as more organisms could thrive in the slightly cooler waters. Oxygen levels in the oceans were variable, and episodes of low oxygen in deeper waters were common.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
At the start of the Ordovician, the supercontinent Gondwana occupied much of the southern hemisphere. It included present-day South America, Africa, Antarctica, Australia, India and Arabia, along with several smaller fragments that would later become parts of southern Europe and Asia. The South Pole lay in what is now North Africa.

Laurentia, comprising most of present-day North America and Greenland, lay on the equator and was surrounded by extensive carbonate platforms. Baltica, the core of northern Europe, was located at temperate southern latitudes, while Siberia lay near the equator. These continents were separated by the Iapetus Ocean and other seaways, and the vast Panthalassic Ocean covered most of the northern hemisphere.

The positions of the continents created distinct faunal provinces, with different animals living in the warm tropical waters around Laurentia and Siberia and in the cooler waters around Baltica and the high-latitude parts of Gondwana. Tectonic activity was increasing, with subduction and island arc volcanism developing along the margins of the Iapetus Ocean and Gondwana.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
During the Early Ordovician, the land surface was still essentially barren of plants, and primary production took place almost entirely in water. Cyanobacteria and other microbes formed mats and stromatolites in shallow seas and tidal flats, and microbial communities, perhaps including fungi and lichen-like associations, probably covered damp areas of the land as thin crusts.

In the oceans, the phytoplankton was dominated by acritarchs, small organic-walled microfossils that are thought to represent the cysts of planktonic algae. Acritarchs began a major diversification during the Early Ordovician, with many new forms bearing elaborate spines and processes. This expansion of the plankton is thought to have provided more food for filter-feeding animals.

Calcareous algae, including green dasycladalean algae and early red algae, grew on carbonate platforms and contributed to the formation of limestones and early reefs. Microbial reefs, built by calcifying cyanobacteria and other microbes together with sponges, were common in tropical seas. The ancestors of land plants, freshwater green algae related to the charophytes, were probably already living in lakes and rivers, but definite land plant spores do not appear until the end of the epoch or the start of the Middle Ordovician.

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
Early Ordovician marine faunas were a mixture of older Cambrian-style animals and newer groups. Trilobites remained very common, with families such as the asaphids becoming especially diverse. Inarticulate and articulate brachiopods, primitive molluscs, sponges and echinoderms lived on the seafloor, and the first bryozoans appeared during this epoch.

Graptolites made the transition from living attached to the seafloor to drifting in the plankton, and planktonic forms such as Rhabdinopora spread rapidly across the world's oceans. Cephalopods began a major radiation, producing a variety of straight and coiled shelled forms that became important predators. Conodonts were also diversifying.

The Fezouata biota of Morocco shows that soft-bodied animals were also abundant. It includes Aegirocassis, a radiodont about two metres long that used comb-like appendages to filter plankton from the water, making it one of the largest animals of its time [4]. Other Fezouata animals include marrellomorph arthropods, lobopodians, early horseshoe crab relatives and armoured animals related to the Cambrian Wiwaxia [2]. Vertebrates were represented by conodonts and possibly early jawless fishes.

sections.heading: Marine Evolution
sections.body:
The Early Ordovician marks the beginning of the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event, a prolonged radiation of marine life that lasted for around 25 million years. Unlike the Cambrian Explosion, which saw the origin of most animal body plans, the Ordovician radiation involved a huge increase in the diversity of species, genera and families within existing groups.

One of the most important changes was the development of a more complex plankton. The diversification of acritarchs, the move of graptolites into the open water, and the radiation of planktonic larvae among many animal groups created new food sources. This in turn supported more filter-feeding animals on the seafloor, such as brachiopods, bryozoans and crinoids, and more predators, such as cephalopods.

The Early Ordovician also saw the beginning of ecological tiering, in which animals lived at different heights above and depths below the seafloor. Burrowing became deeper and more intense, and the first hard surfaces covered with encrusting animals appeared. These changes laid the foundations for the complex marine ecosystems of the rest of the Palaeozoic era.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Late Cambrian, formally known as the Furongian series, was the final epoch of the Cambrian period, lasting from about 497 to 485.4 million years ago. It is divided into the Paibian, Jiangshanian and Stage 10, the last of which has not yet been formally named. The name Furongian comes from the Chinese word for the lotus, a reference to Hunan province in southern China, where key rock sections are found.

The Furongian has sometimes been described as a 'gap' in the history of animal diversity, since it lies between the Cambrian Explosion and the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event. Fossil diversity appears relatively low during this time, though this may partly reflect a scarcity of well-studied fossil sites rather than a genuine absence of life [1].

The Late Cambrian was marked by a series of extinction events among trilobites, known as biomere boundaries, as well as by major disturbances in the carbon cycle. The most famous of these is the Steptoean Positive Carbon Isotope Excursion, or SPICE event, which began near the start of the epoch and is recognised in rocks worldwide [2].

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
The climate of the Late Cambrian was generally hot, with high levels of atmospheric carbon dioxide and no evidence of large polar ice sheets. Tropical sea surface temperatures were probably well above modern values, and warm conditions extended to relatively high latitudes.

The oceans of the Late Cambrian were poorly oxygenated compared with today. Large volumes of deep and intermediate water were anoxic or low in oxygen, and episodes in which this oxygen-poor water spread onto the continental shelves are thought to have caused repeated extinctions of shallow-water trilobites [2]. Some researchers have suggested that each of these extinctions coincided with the arrival of cooler, oxygen-poor water on the shelves.

The SPICE event, beginning around 497 million years ago, involved a large shift in the carbon isotope composition of seawater. It is thought to reflect the burial of large amounts of organic carbon in oxygen-poor sediments, which may in turn have released oxygen into the atmosphere [2, 3]. Some scientists believe the SPICE event led to a significant increase in atmospheric oxygen, which may have helped pave the way for the diversification of life in the Ordovician [3].

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
During the Late Cambrian, the supercontinent Gondwana was the largest landmass on Earth, extending from the equator to high southern latitudes. It included present-day South America, Africa, Antarctica, Australia, India and Arabia, along with fragments of southern Europe, the Middle East and China. Australia and East Antarctica lay in the tropics along the northern margin of Gondwana.

Smaller continents, including Laurentia, Baltica and Siberia, were separated from Gondwana by oceans. Laurentia lay on the equator and was surrounded by broad shallow seas and carbonate platforms, while Baltica lay in cooler southern latitudes. The Iapetus Ocean separated Laurentia from Baltica and Gondwana, and the vast Panthalassic Ocean covered much of the northern hemisphere.

Sea levels were high during much of the Late Cambrian, and large areas of the continents were covered by shallow seas. Sandstones deposited in these seas and along their shorelines are widespread in North America, where some contain trackways and other trace fossils left by arthropods crawling across tidal flats. The land itself was barren, with no plants and only microbial crusts covering damp ground.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
No land plants existed in the Late Cambrian, and the continents were largely barren expanses of rock and sediment. Thin crusts of cyanobacteria, other bacteria, and possibly fungi and simple algae may have covered damp surfaces, helping to stabilise soils and contributing to the weathering of rocks.

In the oceans, the primary producers were cyanobacteria and algae. Acritarchs, the resting cysts of planktonic algae, were common, and Late Cambrian assemblages include forms with complex spines and ornamentation that foreshadow the great acritarch radiation of the Ordovician. Microbial mats were widespread on the seafloor, and stromatolites and thrombolites, layered and clotted structures built by microbes, were especially common in the Late Cambrian.

In fact, the Late Cambrian saw a resurgence of microbial reefs after the decline of the archaeocyathan sponge reefs earlier in the Cambrian. These reefs were built largely by calcifying cyanobacteria such as Girvanella and Epiphyton, along with other microbial communities, and some included the first maceriate reefs, in which small sponges and microbes grew together. Calcareous green and red algae were also present, contributing to the formation of carbonate sediments.

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
Trilobites were the dominant animals of the Late Cambrian seafloor, and they are so common and diverse that they are used to divide the epoch into biozones. However, trilobite faunas were repeatedly devastated by extinction events at the biomere boundaries and then replaced by new forms, often descended from deep-water or cool-water ancestors that migrated onto the shelves.

Other animals included inarticulate brachiopods, sponges, early molluscs, echinoderms and conodonts. The first cephalopods, small animals with chambered shells such as Plectronoceras, appeared in China during the Late Cambrian, beginning a lineage that would later include the giant nautiloids of the Ordovician and the ammonites of the Mesozoic.

Fossils from sites such as the Orsten deposits of Sweden preserve tiny arthropods in exquisite three-dimensional detail, including larval crustaceans and early relatives of the pentastomids. In North America, trackways called Protichnites and Climactichnites suggest that large arthropods and slug-like molluscs ventured onto tidal flats and possibly beyond, perhaps making some of the earliest forays of animals onto land.

sections.heading: Early Arthropods
sections.body:
Arthropods were the most diverse and abundant animals of the Late Cambrian, with trilobites making up the bulk of the fossil record. Trilobites of this time included the olenids, which were adapted to oxygen-poor waters and may have lived in a symbiotic relationship with sulphur-oxidising bacteria [4], and many other groups that lived in shallow, well-oxygenated seas.

The Orsten fossils provide a unique window into the evolution of small arthropods. These microscopic fossils, preserved in phosphate, include early crustaceans, larval stages of various arthropods and animals related to the ancestors of modern groups. They show that crustaceans had already evolved many of their characteristic features, such as specialised limbs for feeding and swimming, by the Late Cambrian.

Large arthropods also left trackways on ancient tidal flats and beaches. Some of these tracks, such as those from the Elk Mound Group of Wisconsin, were probably made by euthycarcinoids, an extinct group of arthropods that may have been related to the ancestors of insects and myriapods. These trackways suggest that arthropods were among the first animals to explore the margins of the land, long before plants had colonised it.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Middle Cambrian, formally known as the Miaolingian series, lasted from about 509 to 497 million years ago. It is divided into three stages: the Wuliuan, the Drumian and the Guzhangian. The name Miaolingian comes from the Miaoling mountains in Guizhou province, China, where important rock sections of this age are exposed [1].

The Middle Cambrian followed the extinction events at the end of the Early Cambrian, which eliminated the reef-building archaeocyathan sponges and many trilobite groups. During this time, marine ecosystems continued to develop in the wake of the Cambrian Explosion, and trilobites diversified to become the most prominent animals of the seafloor.

The Middle Cambrian is best known for the Burgess Shale of British Columbia, Canada, one of the most famous fossil sites in the world. Discovered by Charles Walcott in 1909, it preserves a remarkable variety of soft-bodied animals, including many strange creatures that do not fit easily into modern groups. Other important sites of this age include the Kaili biota of China and the Wheeler Shale of Utah.

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
The Middle Cambrian climate was generally warm, with high levels of atmospheric carbon dioxide, perhaps more than ten times the modern level. There is little evidence of glaciation, and warm conditions appear to have extended to relatively high latitudes. Tropical sea surface temperatures were probably higher than today.

The oceans of the Middle Cambrian were less well oxygenated than modern oceans, and large areas of deep water were probably anoxic. Episodes of low oxygen sometimes spread into shallower waters, and some extinction events among trilobites have been linked to these changes. The Drumian Carbon Isotope Excursion, or DICE, which occurred near the start of the Drumian stage, was accompanied by trilobite extinctions and may reflect such disturbances.

Sea levels were generally high and rising during this epoch, flooding the edges of the continents and creating extensive shallow marine environments. Thick carbonate deposits accumulated on platforms in tropical regions, while fine muds settled in deeper basins. The Burgess Shale itself was formed in deep water at the foot of a towering limestone reef escarpment, where mudflows periodically buried animals living on the seafloor.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
During the Middle Cambrian, the largest landmass was the supercontinent Gondwana, which had formed at the end of the Precambrian. It comprised present-day South America, Africa, Antarctica, Australia, India and Arabia, along with fragments that would later form parts of southern Europe, the Middle East and China. Much of eastern Gondwana, including Australia, lay in the tropics.

Several smaller continents lay separately from Gondwana. Laurentia, which included most of present-day North America, straddled the equator and was surrounded by extensive carbonate platforms. The Burgess Shale was deposited on the western margin of Laurentia, which faced the vast Panthalassic Ocean. Baltica lay in temperate southern latitudes, while Siberia lay near the equator.

The Iapetus Ocean separated Laurentia, Baltica and Gondwana, and it was growing wider as these continents moved apart. High sea levels flooded the low-lying margins of the continents, creating broad shallow seas in which most Cambrian animals lived. The continental interiors were barren, with no plants to bind soils, so rivers were broad and braided and carried large quantities of sand into the seas.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
There were no land plants during the Middle Cambrian, and the continents were largely barren. Microbial crusts of cyanobacteria and other organisms probably covered moist ground in places, and they may have played a role in weathering rocks and forming primitive soils.

In the oceans, the primary producers were cyanobacteria and algae. Acritarchs, the fossilised cysts of planktonic algae, were common and formed an important part of the plankton. Middle Cambrian acritarchs include a variety of spiny and ornamented forms that were more complex than those of earlier times.

Algae are also preserved in the Burgess Shale and other sites of exceptional preservation. These include filamentous and branching forms such as Dalyia, which is thought to be a green alga, and Marpolia, which may have been a cyanobacterium; Margaretia, long considered a green alga, is now interpreted as the tube of a hemichordate [2]. Microbial mats were still common on the seafloor, though they were becoming less widespread as burrowing and grazing animals disturbed the sediment. Stromatolites and microbial reefs, built by calcifying cyanobacteria such as Epiphyton and Renalcis, were important in shallow tropical seas after the disappearance of archaeocyathan sponge reefs.

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
The fauna of the Middle Cambrian is known in remarkable detail thanks to the Burgess Shale and similar deposits. Arthropods were the most diverse animals, including trilobites and many other forms such as Marrella, the most common animal in the Burgess Shale, and the large predator Anomalocaris, a radiodont that could reach about a metre in length.

Other animals included sponges, such as Vauxia; priapulid worms, such as Ottoia; polychaete worms; and the lobopodian Hallucigenia, a strange worm-like animal with spines on its back and legs below. Wiwaxia was a slug-like animal covered in scales and spines, and Opabinia had five eyes and a long, flexible proboscis ending in a grasping claw. Echinoderms, brachiopods and early molluscs were also present.

Chordates were represented by Pikaia, a small, swimming animal with a notochord and segmented muscles, which is related to the ancestors of vertebrates. Metaspriggina, a primitive jawless fish from the Burgess Shale, shows that true vertebrates were already present [3]. The Middle Cambrian also saw the rise of agnostid trilobites, tiny blind arthropods that may have lived in the plankton and are valuable for correlating rocks around the world.

sections.heading: Early Arthropods
sections.body:
The Middle Cambrian provides a remarkable picture of early arthropod evolution. Trilobites were the most common arthropods with hard skeletons, and they diversified into a wide range of forms, from tiny agnostids to large species such as Paradoxides, which could exceed 30 centimetres in length. Thousands of trilobite fossils from sites such as the Wheeler Shale of Utah have made Elrathia kingii one of the most familiar fossils in the world.

The Burgess Shale reveals many soft-bodied arthropods that are not preserved elsewhere. These include Marrella, a small arthropod with long spines on its head; Canadaspis, an early relative of crustaceans; Sidneyia, a predator with a broad, flattened body; and Waptia, a shrimp-like animal that has been found with eggs attached to its body, showing that it cared for its young [4].

The Burgess Shale also preserves animals that illuminate the origins of arthropods. Radiodonts such as Anomalocaris and Hurdia, and the lobopodian Opabinia, belong to the 'stem group' of arthropods, meaning they branched off before the evolution of the hard, jointed exoskeletons and legs of true arthropods. These animals show how features such as compound eyes, segmented limbs and hard body coverings evolved step by step.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Early Cambrian, comprising the Terreneuvian and Series 2 epochs, lasted from about 538.8 to 509 million years ago. It marks the beginning of the Cambrian period, the Palaeozoic era and the Phanerozoic eon, the eon of 'visible life'. Its base is defined by the first appearance of the trace fossil Treptichnus pedum at Fortune Head in Newfoundland, Canada, which records the burrowing of complex animals [1].

The Early Cambrian was the time of the Cambrian Explosion, a remarkable episode of evolution in which most major groups of animals appeared in the fossil record over a period of around 20 to 25 million years. During this time, animals developed hard skeletons, eyes, legs and complex behaviours, and the first food webs based on active predation took shape.

The Early Cambrian is known from several sites of exceptional preservation, most notably the Chengjiang biota of Yunnan, China, and the Sirius Passet fauna of Greenland, both around 518 million years old. These sites preserve soft-bodied animals in remarkable detail, providing a unique insight into the earliest animal communities.
