sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
The climate of the Early Cambrian was generally warm, with high levels of atmospheric carbon dioxide and little or no polar ice. This was a sharp contrast to the Cryogenian period earlier in the Neoproterozoic, when the Earth experienced repeated 'snowball' glaciations. Tropical sea surface temperatures were probably higher than today.

Oxygen levels in the atmosphere and oceans had risen during the late Neoproterozoic, and they appear to have fluctuated during the Early Cambrian. Many scientists believe that rising oxygen levels were an important factor in the Cambrian Explosion, since larger and more active animals require more oxygen. However, the deep oceans remained largely anoxic, and oxygen-poor water periodically spread onto the continental shelves.

The chemistry of seawater was also changing. Rising sea levels flooded the continents and increased the amount of calcium, phosphorus and other elements in seawater, which may have helped animals to build mineralised skeletons [2]. The Early Cambrian closed with a series of extinction events, including the Sinsk event around 513 million years ago, linked to the spread of oxygen-poor waters, which wiped out the archaeocyathan sponge reefs and many early trilobites [3].

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
During the Early Cambrian, the continents were arranged quite differently from today. The supercontinent Gondwana, which had assembled during the Pan-African orogeny at the end of the Precambrian, was the largest landmass. It comprised present-day South America, Africa, Antarctica, Australia, India and Arabia, and it stretched from the equator to high southern latitudes.

Several smaller continents lay separate from Gondwana, including Laurentia, Baltica and Siberia. These had broken away from the earlier supercontinent Rodinia during the Neoproterozoic, and they were now separated by young and growing oceans, including the Iapetus Ocean. South China and North China were located near the margins of Gondwana in the tropics, and the Chengjiang biota was deposited in shallow seas on the South China block.

Sea levels rose dramatically during the Early Cambrian, flooding the margins of the continents and creating extensive shallow seas. This marine transgression, which deposited widespread sandstones and limestones, has left a remarkable surface called the Great Unconformity in many parts of the world, where Cambrian rocks lie directly on much older eroded Precambrian rocks [2].

image.caption: Basal Cambrian GSSP at Fortune Head, Newfoundland

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
There were no plants on land during the Early Cambrian, and the continents were largely barren. However, microbial communities of cyanobacteria, other bacteria and perhaps fungi or simple algae probably formed thin crusts on damp surfaces, contributing to weathering and the earliest soils.

In the oceans, photosynthesis was carried out by cyanobacteria and algae. Acritarchs, the microscopic fossilised cysts of planktonic algae, underwent a major diversification during the Early Cambrian, with new forms bearing spines and other ornaments. This diversification may have been linked to the rise of planktonic grazers, which put pressure on algae to develop defences.

Microbial mats were widespread on the seafloor at the start of the Cambrian, as they had been during the Ediacaran period, but they declined as burrowing animals began to churn up the sediment in a process known as the Cambrian substrate revolution. Calcifying cyanobacteria, such as Epiphyton and Renalcis, formed microbial reefs together with archaeocyathan sponges in shallow tropical seas. Seaweeds, including early green and red algae, were also present, and some are preserved in the Chengjiang biota.

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
The earliest part of the Cambrian, the Terreneuvian, is characterised by the 'small shelly fauna', a collection of tiny mineralised tubes, cones, scales and plates produced by a variety of early animals, including molluscs, brachiopods and armoured worm-like animals. Trace fossils also became more complex as animals began to burrow deeper into the sediment.

The first trilobites appeared around 521 million years ago, and they rapidly diversified to become some of the most common animals of the Cambrian. Archaeocyathans, a group of sponges with cup-shaped skeletons, built the first animal reefs. The Chengjiang and Sirius Passet biotas reveal a wide variety of soft-bodied animals, including arthropods, sponges, worms, lobopodians, early echinoderms and chordates.

Chordates are represented in the Chengjiang biota by animals such as Myllokunmingia and Haikouichthys, which are among the earliest known vertebrates [4]. These small, fish-like animals had a skull-like structure, gills and a dorsal fin. Other notable animals include Yunnanozoon, the vetulicolians, and the predatory radiodonts, such as Amplectobelua, which were the largest animals of their time, reaching lengths of up to a metre.

image.caption: Myllokunmingia fengjiaoa, an early vertebrate (Nobu Tamura)

sections.heading: Animal Origins
sections.body:
The Early Cambrian was the time of the Cambrian Explosion, during which representatives of most living animal phyla appeared in the fossil record. Although molecular clock studies suggest that many animal groups originated earlier in the Neoproterozoic, the Cambrian saw a rapid increase in the diversity, size and complexity of animals, as well as the first widespread appearance of hard skeletons.

The causes of the Cambrian Explosion are still debated. Possible factors include rising oxygen levels, which allowed animals to grow larger and more active; changes in seawater chemistry, which made it easier to build skeletons [2]; and the evolution of new genetic tools for building complex bodies, such as the Hox genes. Ecological factors were also important, particularly the rise of predation, which led to an 'arms race' between predators and prey and favoured the evolution of armour, spines, eyes and burrowing.

Arthropods were among the most important animals of the Cambrian Explosion. Chengjiang fossils include early arthropods such as Fuxianhuia, which preserves traces of a brain and nervous system, and many other forms related to modern groups. Eyes, including the compound eyes of trilobites and radiodonts, evolved early and may have helped drive the explosion by making predators more effective hunters.
